      Welcome to the Platinum+ Wiki

      The definitive wiki to configure your computer from start to finish, in a way that is accessible to anyone and free of charge, offering the end user the maximum performance possible.

      Get started with the program Start with Windows setup

      Why this Wiki?

      I created this wiki to make it available to anyone looking to configure and optimize their computer for maximum potential and long-term efficiency. The goal is to eliminate both hardware and software resource waste while avoiding so-called "tweaks" (paid or otherwise) that promise miraculous improvements but only end up compromising system stability or, worse, wearing out hardware components over time.

      This guide is designed to be accessible to everyone, from power users to those with only basic computer knowledge, helping them set up their machines from start to finish in an efficient and intuitive way. I want users to be truly in control of their systems—including from a security perspective—without having to make unnecessary compromises.

      Ultimately, the objective is for everyone to be fully aware of the changes they make to their PC, clearly understanding every risk and every benefit.

      Work in Progress: This guide is under continuous development. If you have any doubts or want to help me improve the content, you can contact me privately on social media or write to us directly in the Discord community. Every contribution to the project is welcome!
      Last modified: July 6, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      What is Platinum+ Optimizer?

      Platinum+ Optimizer (also known as Project-Platinum) is a completely free and open-source project, available on GitHub and Discord. It is a collection of documented guides and tutorials, along with its own graphical user interface tool, designed with one main goal: to give users maximum control over their machine and full awareness of everything running on their computer. It allows users to customize and configure the Windows operating system from scratch based on their preferences and their PC hardware specifications.

      The program allows users to remove unnecessary components and software, improving system responsiveness, reducing background activity, and increasing performance by freeing up valuable system resources.

      It also provides access to a wide range of fully documented hardware and system optimizations. Users can optimize Windows for gaming, low latency, responsiveness, power efficiency, stability, and general everyday use.

      Unlike "meaningless automatic optimizers," Platinum+ Optimizer allows users to modify advanced Windows settings with just a few clicks thanks to its simplified interface and related tutorials. Every parameter is explained and documented, including its benefits and recommended usage scenarios.

      The project focuses on transparency and user awareness. The software does not silently apply automatic modifications or optimizations. Every tweak, change, and optimization must be applied manually by the user, ensuring full control over the operating system.

      Platinum+ Optimizer also includes a restore and recovery system. Users can quickly revert changes manually or through the built-in recovery tools. This allows safe experimentation with system optimizations and makes it possible to restore configurations, settings, or behaviors whenever necessary.

      The program also includes a dedicated security and recovery section. Any applied modification can be reverted, providing safety, reliability, and peace of mind, especially when experimenting with advanced configurations.

      The tool is written in PowerShell, meaning the source code is readable, transparent, and easy to inspect. Users can clearly see which operations the program performs on the system. No hidden automation or silent background behavior.

      Last modified: July 14, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      How to use this Wiki

      This wiki has been designed to be as intuitive and efficient as possible. Before diving into the guides, take a few minutes to familiarise yourself with the interface — it will save you a lot of time and make your experience significantly smoother.

      Interface Overview

      The wiki is divided into three main areas that are always visible on screen:

      Left Sidebar

      The navigation menu. Contains all chapters and sub-sections of the wiki, organised in a collapsible tree. Click any section header to expand it and reveal its pages.

      Main Content Area

      The central reading panel where all guide content is displayed. Each page contains step-by-step instructions, screenshots, alerts, and code blocks.

      Right TOC Panel

      Table of Contents — dynamically generated for each page. Click any heading to instantly jump to that section within the current article. The active heading is automatically highlighted as you scroll.

      Navigating with the Sidebar

      The left sidebar contains the full table of contents for the wiki, structured as a collapsible tree with two levels of depth:

      1 Main Chapters

      Top-level items (e.g. 2. Operating System, 3. Post-Setup OS) represent the major chapters of the wiki. Click the chapter header to expand or collapse all the sub-sections within it.

      2 Sub-Sections

      Inside each chapter, you'll find sub-sections (e.g. 2.1 Preparation Phase, 2.3 Bootable USB). These can also be expanded individually to reveal the specific pages inside.

      3 Pages

      Clicking on a page link inside a sub-section loads that guide in the main content area. The active page is always highlighted in blue in the sidebar so you always know where you are.

      Auto-expand on Navigation When you click a search result or follow a direct link to a page, the sidebar automatically opens the relevant chapter and sub-section for you — you never have to hunt for the page manually.

      The Documentation Button

      Throughout the wiki, you may notice a Documentation button appearing at the top of certain pages or sections. Clicking it opens a side panel with the full technical explanation of that topic — why a setting works the way it does, what happens under the hood, and the reasoning behind each recommendation. It is aimed at users who want to understand the why behind a procedure, not just follow the steps. If you just want to get the job done, you can safely ignore it and follow the main guide as normal.

      Using the Search Bar

      The search bar at the top of the page is one of the most powerful tools in the wiki. It lets you find any content — across every chapter and every step — in real time. Click the search bar in the header, or press the / key from anywhere on the page to instantly focus it. As you type, matching results appear grouped by category — click any of them to jump directly to that section with the searched word highlighted on screen.

      Language Selector

      The wiki supports translation into over 100 languages via the language selector in the top-right corner of the header. Click the globe icon and select your preferred language from the dropdown. The entire wiki content will be automatically translated.

      Powered by Google Translate Translation is handled automatically by Google Translate. While it covers the vast majority of languages accurately, some technical terms may not translate perfectly. The original English version is always the most precise reference.

      Operating System Selection

      Before proceeding with the installation and complete reconfiguration, we must choose which operating system to install on our computer. Today we only have two choices: Windows 10 and Windows 11.

      This decision should not be based solely on graphical preferences or habits, but on concrete technical criteria such as hardware compatibility, system requirements, level of software support, and performance optimization.

      In a modern context, the choice of the operating system directly affects the system's stability, security, and overall performance. For this reason, it is important to carefully evaluate the characteristics of both environments.

      Step 1: Evaluating the operating systems

      Windows 10 Windows 10 runs better on older hardware because it is lighter, uses fewer resources, and has fewer useless background programs (bloatware). This makes it faster and more responsive than newer systems, ensuring a smoother experience even on less powerful PCs.

      The life cycle of Windows 10 is now complete. Official Microsoft support ended in October 2025. Since then, the system no longer receives feature or security updates. Using Windows 10 connected to the internet requires great care. Any new threats or vulnerabilities will no longer be addressed automatically.

      However, if your computer does not meet the requirements to install Windows 11, Windows 10 remains the only viable choice for older hardware. To use it more safely, we recommend using a reliable third-party antivirus like Malwarebytes. Also, keep your browser and essential programs updated. Adopt safe browsing habits, avoiding unverified downloads or sites. It is the mandatory choice for those with an old PC that doesn't support the new system. However, it must be used with awareness and additional protections, keeping in mind that it will no longer receive updates.
      Windows 11 Windows 11 is the current platform. It receives constant security and feature updates. It is designed to make the best use of the latest hardware. It manages modern processors more efficiently and takes full advantage of SSD speeds. It optimizes memory usage, ensuring a smoother experience and faster response times.

      Built-in protections work in the background without weighing down the computer. The interface has been simplified to make daily operations more intuitive. If your PC was produced in recent years or has recent components, using Windows 11 is the best choice. Not only will you get more consistent performance and an always-protected system, but you will also ensure greater longevity for your device, keeping it compatible with today's applications, games, and security standards.

      Step 2: What hardware do I have and what operating system am I currently using?

      To view all the specifications of the computer, we will use "System Information", a built-in Windows tool that provides detailed information about the system and installed hardware components. This program is identified by the executable file msinfo32.exe.

      Step 1

      To open it, press the "Start" button and type "System Information" in the search bar. Once you find the program, click on "Run as administrator".

      Step 2

      After launching it, a window will appear showing a complete overview of the computer. From here, you can view information such as the system model, installed processor, amount of RAM, BIOS or UEFI version, operating system, and many other useful details. Refer to the image below to identify the main information to note.

      Step 3

      If you want to view more detailed information about the graphics card, expand the "Components" section in the left panel and then select "Display". In this section, you will find the graphics card model, installed driver version, available video memory, and other details related to the system's graphics subsystem.

      Step 3: Which operating system to choose for your hardware

      I've created a series of questions to figure out which system is best suited based on the hardware.

      Component Your Hardware Recommendation Key Reason
      Memory (RAM)
      		4 GB or less Windows 10 Lighter system load, keeps older hardware responsive and highly stable.
      6 GB or more Proceed to CPU Check Meets the baseline memory requirements for a modern operating system.
      Processor (CPU)
      		Intel Core 1st - 7th Gen
      or AMD Ryzen 1000 & older       		Windows 10 Official Windows 11 requirement starts at Intel 8th Gen / AMD Ryzen 2000.
      Intel 8th Gen or newer
      or AMD Ryzen 2000 & newer       		Proceed to Disk Check Fully compatible with security standards and multi-thread hardware optimizations.
      Storage Drive
      		Mechanical HDD Windows 10 Windows 11 is highly optimized for fast random reads and runs sluggishly on mechanical drives.
      Solid State Drive (SSD) Windows 11 Recommended choice! Take advantage of DirectStorage, advanced security, and full support.

      Windows Stock vs LTSC Comparison

      Before proceeding with system installation and tuning, it is critical to understand the architectural differences between standard consumer editions of Windows and the Enterprise LTSC (Long-Term Servicing Channel) releases. Your choice of edition establishes the absolute baseline for all subsequent optimizations.

      Understanding Windows Editions

      Both Windows Stock and LTSC are official, unmodified operating systems provided directly by Microsoft, but their design philosophies and resource management behaviors are drastically different.

      1 Windows Stock (Home or Pro)

      The standard consumer and commercial release. It is fully featured but comes saturated with built-in applications, Microsoft services, telemetry, and aggressive background update mechanisms. While it offers seamless out-of-the-box compatibility with the entire Microsoft ecosystem, it is inherently bloated. The system utilizes a significant amount of RAM, CPU cycles, and disk I/O simply to sustain background tasks, UWP apps, and forced feature integrations.

      2 Windows LTSC (Long-Term Servicing Channel)

      A specialized, enterprise-grade edition designed for mission-critical environments where absolute stability and low resource overhead are mandatory. It is a minimal, official version of Windows shipped entirely stripped of consumer bloatware. It removes most consumer-facing components such as preinstalled UWP apps, Xbox services, and optional Microsoft consumer features. The result is a highly optimized operating system with a drastically lighter footprint, significantly fewer active background processes, and uncompromised stability.

      Windows 10: Stock vs LTSC 2021

      If your hardware configuration or personal preference dictates that Windows 10 is the appropriate choice, we absolutely recommend using Windows 10 LTSC 2021 over any Stock edition.

      From a strict technical standpoint, Windows 10 version 21H2 (the foundation of LTSC 2021) and the final Windows 10 version 22H2 share the same underlying system base and servicing branch architecture. Because the underlying architecture is identical, raw performance is virtually indistinguishable between the two. There is no real-world performance advantage or optimization benefit to running the 22H2 build.

      Why LTSC 2021 is Superior for Tuning

      LTSC 2021 is vastly superior for system tuning for several reasons:

      Drastically Reduced Overhead: Lower DPC latency, reduced input lag, and improved system responsiveness due to fewer background processes.

      Update Control: The LTSC branch is engineered to receive only critical security patches, bypassing the continuous, often system-breaking feature updates pushed to Stock versions.

      Extreme Tuning: For users building a strictly offline or highly isolated gaming rig who are not concerned with advanced security rollouts, Windows Update can be safely and permanently disabled without compromising the core integrity of the operating system.

      Windows 10 Resource Usage Comparison

      Windows 10 Stock

      Windows 10 LTSC

      Windows 11: Stock vs. LTSC

      Windows 11 LTSC follows the same minimal, enterprise-grade philosophy but is built upon Microsoft's most modern architecture. It features an updated thread scheduler designed to efficiently manage modern multi-core processors (such as Intel's Big.Little architecture) and takes full advantage of high-speed storage technologies like DirectStorage.

      However, the baseline of Windows 11 is fundamentally heavier than Windows 10. Consequently, Windows 11 LTSC is less "minimal" than its Windows 10 counterpart. It still removes the consumer bloatware found in Windows 11 Stock, making it the best way to run Microsoft's latest OS, but it inherently utilizes more system resources than Windows 10 LTSC.

      Windows 11 LTSC is an excellent, highly stable choice for recent, high-end hardware configurations. However, it is less ideal for older PCs or machines where ultra-optimization and absolute minimal resource usage are the primary goals.

      Important Consideration Windows 11 LTSC is excellent for recent, high-end hardware configurations but less ideal for older PCs or machines where ultra-optimization and absolute minimal resource usage are the primary goals. For maximum performance, Windows 10 LTSC remains the superior choice.

      System Preparation

      If you have decided to format the PC, you must keep in mind that all your data and applications will be deleted. For this reason, you have three options:

      1. Complete Backup

      Back up your data, saving it on an external storage device or on a cloud service like Google Drive.

      2. Dual Boot

      Consider using a dual boot setup, based on available disk space, to gradually transfer data from one system to another.

      3. Secondary Drive

      Use a secondary drive (not external USB drives) on which to perform a clean installation. It is recommended that it has the same or higher read/write performance.

      Step 1: Tools required for formatting

      Before starting the procedure and before downloading the operating system ISO file, we must make sure we have a working USB flash drive of at least 8GB.

      Step 2: How do I check the storage space?

      1 Insertion

      Insert the USB flash drive into the computer as shown in the picture.

      2 Verify space

      Open File Explorer and check the total space of the newly inserted flash drive (Recommended 8GB).

      Last modified: July 6, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Identify Disk Partition Style (MBR/GPT)

      Before creating your bootable USB drive, you need to identify the partition style of your current hard drive or SSD. This ensures that you choose the correct configuration in Rufus (MBR or GPT) to avoid installation errors and guarantee that the system boots correctly on your motherboard.

      Why is this important?
      • GPT (GUID Partition Table): The modern standard. It is required if your motherboard uses UEFI mode, if you want to install Windows 11, or if your drive is larger than 2TB.
      • MBR (Master Boot Record): The legacy standard. Used for older systems operating in legacy BIOS mode.

      Step 1

      Right-click on the Windows logo (Start button) in the taskbar and select Disk Management from the power user menu.

      Step 2

      In the Disk Management window, locate the disk where your operating system is currently installed (usually Disk 0). Right-click on the disk name (on the left panel, not the partitions block) and select Properties.

      Step 3

      In the Properties window, navigate to the Volumes tab. Look for the Partition style entry under the Disk Information section to see if it is listed as GUID Partition Table (GPT) or Master Boot Record (MBR).

      This guide covers configuring and creating a bootable USB drive for Windows 10 or Windows 11 using Rufus. If you have not downloaded the software yet, please refer to the previous guide. Please pay close attention to the two expandable dropdown sections (popups) located below on this page, which are dedicated to Windows 10 and Windows 11 respectively. It is critical that you open and expand only the section corresponding to the specific operating system version you intend to install. Carefully following all the steps outlined within the correct dropdown is essential to prevent compatibility issues and ensure a successful installation process.

      Complete step-by-step walkthrough for configuring Rufus with a Windows 10 ISO image. Make sure to plug in a USB flash drive with at least 8GB capacity (note that all data on it will be deleted!).

      Step 1

      Open File Explorer and launch the program by right-clicking it and selecting "Run as administrator."

      Step 2

      This is the Rufus interface: verify that your USB flash drive is correctly inserted into the computer and selected in the "Device" section. Once verified, click "Select."

      Step 3

      Select the newly downloaded file; in my case for Windows 10, the file will usually be located in the Documents folder or the folder you chose during the download, then click "Open."

      Step 4

      Leave the settings as recommended by Rufus, but pay close attention to the "Partition scheme" section. As shown in the previous section (Identify Disk Partition Style), if your drive is GPT, select GPT; if it is MBR, select MBR.

      Step 5

      Accept any popups (in my case, Rufus warns that the Windows 10 ISO contains a revoked UEFI bootloader, meaning it's no longer considered secure by Secure Boot). This can cause boot errors on PCs with Secure Boot enabled, so it's recommended to use an updated ISO or disable Secure Boot in the BIOS/UEFI. Because of this, you might need to disable Secure Boot later on if you haven't already.

      Step 6

      Important Note If you want full system customization and plan to create a custom XML file, you can skip all options in this Rufus ISO customization popup and still continue with creating the bootable USB. You can refer to the next section to learn more. In this case, make sure to wait before proceeding with the installation.

      Here you'll find a few ISO customization options, such as pre-creating a local account and skipping the privacy questions. My advice is to select all three of them, so you get a more automated, clean installation with an account that is already set up with your name and regional preferences.

      Step 7

      A pop-up warning will appear stating that all data on the flash drive will be formatted. I take no responsibility for accidentally formatted USB drives. Before proceeding, please verify that the drive does not contain any useful or important files; once you have verified this, click 'OK'.

      Step 8

      Wait for the ISO files to be successfully copied to the flash drive without touching it, ejecting it, or closing the program.

      Step 9

      Once the process is complete, make sure the word "READY" appears at the bottom. At that point, you can close the program, but do not eject the flash drive from the computer just yet.

      XML Customization (Unattended Setup)

      Before proceeding with standard Windows installation screens, you can automate and customize the entire setup phase using an answer file. This file, typically named autounattend.xml, allows you to skip repetitive setup screens, bypass default requirements, and pre-configure system settings.

      An XML configuration file (autounattend.xml or unattend.xml) is a structured configuration file that the Windows Setup engine reads during boot. It acts as an automated answer sheet for the questions Windows typically asks you during the initial installation process and the Out-of-Box Experience (OOBE).

      By using an unattended XML file, you can pre-define essential settings. It automates the creation of local user accounts with specific names and passwords, bypassing the manual setup. It configures regional settings, keyboard layouts, timezones, and language options automatically.

      It also manages privacy configurations by disabling diagnostic data collection, advertising IDs, and location tracking from the first boot. Furthermore, it allows you to skip the forced Microsoft account sign-in requirements and bypass hardware checks like TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, and minimum RAM requirements.

      During boot, the Windows Installer automatically searches specific locations for a file named autounattend.xml. The most common placement is the root directory of your bootable USB drive. Alternatively, tools like Rufus can inject similar configurations during the USB creation process based on the selections you make in its interface.

      Generating and Using your XML File

      This unattended customization method is fully compatible with both Windows 10 and Windows 11 installations. The generator tool allows you to tailor the configuration file to the specific requirements of either operating system, ensuring a consistent setup experience regardless of the version you choose.

      Manually writing XML code from scratch can be complex and prone to syntax errors. You can generate a customized, clean configuration file using structured web utilities.

      Step 1

      Open any search engine and type "Generate autounattend.xml files for Windows 10/11", then click the first result.

      Step 2

      This utility provides a visual interface where you can select exactly which features to enable or disable. You can configure options to bypass Windows 11 hardware checks, disable telemetry, or pre-configure a local user account.

      Go through the options carefully and configure them according to your hardware specifications and preferences.

      Step 3

      Once you have finished configuring your options, scroll to the bottom of the generator page and click the download link to save the generated file to your computer, making sure it is named exactly autounattend.xml.

      Step 4

      Plug in your bootable USB drive created with Rufus or the Media Creation Tool, then open File Explorer and navigate to the root directory of the drive where the setup.exe file and sources folder are located.

      Copy and paste your autounattend.xml file directly into this root directory without placing it inside any subfolders. If Rufus's built-in customization options were used, it may have already generated a basic automation file, which will be overwritten by your custom autounattend.xml configuration.

      Last modified: July 12, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      USB Boot Procedure

      Once your bootable USB is successfully created, the next crucial step is to boot your computer from it. This instructs the motherboard BIOS/UEFI firmware to load the Windows installation environment rather than your current operating system.

      Boot Mode Tip Modern systems should always be booted in UEFI mode. Make sure UEFI mode is enabled in your BIOS settings and CSM (Compatibility Support Module / Legacy Boot) is disabled for maximum compatibility and modern feature support.

      Motherboard Boot Menu Hotkeys

      To trigger the boot device selection menu without changing permanent BIOS settings, restart your computer and repeatedly tap the appropriate hotkey as soon as the screen turns on.

      Motherboard / PC Manufacturer Boot Menu Hotkey
      ASUS F8
      Gigabyte F12
      MSI F11
      ASRock F11
      Dell F12
      Lenovo F12 / Fn + F12
      HP F10 / Esc
      Acer F12 / Esc

      Step-by-Step Boot Procedure

      1 Identify and enter the BIOS

      To boot from the USB drive and start the installation, we first need to know how to enter the BIOS and set the USB drive as the primary boot device. First, we must identify the motherboard brand, which usually appears on the screen as soon as we turn on the computer (in my case, with a Gigabyte, it even tells me the key combination to enter the BIOS). If we don't know the key combination to enter the BIOS, we can search for the manufacturer's name followed by "bios key" on a search engine to find the correct key. Finally, we restart the computer and, as soon as the manufacturer's logo appears, we repeatedly press that key to access the BIOS.

      2 Boot from the USB drive

      To boot from the USB flash drive, we need to go to the section of the BIOS typically called Boot and set the USB drive as the primary boot device (First Boot Device). If you selected the GPT format in Rufus, choose the flash drive with the UEFI label in the boot menu. If you selected MBR instead, choose the flash drive without the UEFI label.

      3 Save changes and restart

      Apply the changes by pressing the dedicated key to save and restart the computer.

      Windows 10 Setup

      This guide is dedicated to installing Windows 10 using a USB flash drive. Keep in mind that we will have to definitively decide whether to format the drive using diskpart or install the OS on a different partition.

      Disclaimer I take no responsibility for accidentally formatted drives. This wiki explains in detail how to completely format the C: drive. If you want to install Windows on another partition instead, or if you don't want to take any risks, hit us up on Discord!

      Step 1

      Wait for the USB drive to load until the setup appears. Choose the language, time and currency format, and keyboard input method according to your preferences, then click "Next".

      Step 2

      Click on the "Install now" button.

      Step 3

      If you have a Windows license, you can enter it here and then click "Next". If you have previously activated Windows with a digital license, or if you don't have a license, you can click directly on "I don't have a product key" to continue.

      Step 4

      Choose the Windows edition. For LTSC, select "Windows 10 IoT Enterprise LTSC" to have the minimal, enterprise-grade experience.

      Step 5

      Accept the license terms and continue by clicking "Next".

      Step 6

      Click on the "Custom: Install Windows only (advanced)" button to manage the installation and decide where and how to install Windows cleanly.

      Step 7

      Here we have the disk section: if you planned a dual boot or an installation on an already clean secondary disk, select the empty partition you created and click "Next". In the case of a disk to be formatted, go to the next step.

      Step 8

      If you need to completely format the primary drive, erasing all data and partitions, press SHIFT + F10 during setup to open the Command Prompt.

      Follow the instructions in the next steps carefully and precisely to avoid mistakes.

      Step 9

      Type the following command and press Enter to open the specific disk management tool:

      diskpart

      Step 10

      Type the following command and press Enter to display all drives (hard drives, SSDs, USB drives) currently connected to the computer:

      list disk

      Step 11

      Once identified, type the following command (replace 0 with your drive number, if different) and press Enter:

      select disk 0

      Step 12

      WARNING: This command will permanently delete all data, files, and partitions on the selected drive. Make 100% sure you have selected the correct drive.

      Type the following command and press Enter to wipe the drive:

      clean

      Step 13

      Once the cleanup is complete, you can close the Command Prompt window (by clicking the X or typing exit).

      Step 14

      Return to the Windows Setup screen, click Refresh to reload the drive list, and select the newly wiped unallocated space to proceed with the installation.

      Step 15

      Now carefully select the newly formatted drive where Windows 10 LTSC will be permanently installed. Make sure to choose the correct one.

      Step 16

      Wait until the installation is finished without touching or ejecting the USB drive, and without canceling the installation.

      Step 17

      As soon as it finishes, click the "Restart Now" button at the bottom. Right after the restart, you can manually eject the USB drive to prevent the PC from entering the Windows setup again. Alternatively, set the Windows Boot Manager as the primary boot option in the BIOS.

      Step 18

      Wait for the system to boot up and configure itself automatically, without turning off the computer or performing other operations.

      Step 19

      Next up is the initial Windows setup (OOBE). For LTSC, the setup process is streamlined and will skip many consumer-focused screens. If it asks you to set up your network, just connect with an Ethernet cable or select your Wi-Fi network and enter the password. If you don't have a connection available, you can simply select "I don't have internet" to set it up later.

      Need help? If you run into any issues during this step, feel free to reach out to us privately for support!

      Step 20

      Wait for the user login to process.

      Step 21

      Verify that you have successfully entered the PC without encountering any errors. Then proceed through the next sections to complete the configuration and continue the optimization process.

      Choose Connection Type

      Before we begin with the rest of the configuration, we must ensure your internet connection is active. If you have already configured your network during the initial Windows OOBE (Out-of-Box Experience) or have already set it up manually, you can safely skip this step and proceed to the next section of the wiki.

      If you haven't configured your connection yet, you must do so now to continue. To provide you with the correct instructions, please select the option below that matches the type of connection you are using (Wired Ethernet or Wireless Wi-Fi):

      Complete step-by-step walkthrough for setting up your wired Ethernet connection. Make sure your network cable is securely plugged into both your PC and your router or modem to ensure a stable and reliable connection.

      Step 1

      Ensure one end of your Ethernet cable is firmly plugged into your PC's network port and the other end is connected to your router or modem.

      Step 2

      Windows is designed to automatically detect wired connections; if the cable is functional and the router is providing a signal, your PC should establish a connection immediately without further input. To confirm that the connection is active, look at the bottom-right corner of your taskbar, where the network icon should appear as a small computer monitor, indicating an active Ethernet connection.

      Step 3

      If you have no internet access, navigate to Settings > Network & internet > Ethernet. Ensure the status is set to "Connected". If it shows "Unidentified network" or no connection, verify the cable integrity or check your router settings.

      Complete step-by-step walkthrough for setting up your wireless Wi-Fi connection. Make sure you have your network name (SSID) and security key (Wi-Fi password) readily available before you begin the setup process.

      Step 1

      Click on the network icon located in the bottom-right corner of your taskbar (near the clock).

      Step 2

      If the Wi-Fi button is greyed out or off, click it once to turn it on.

      Step 3

      A list of available wireless networks will appear; select the SSID of your home or office network, then click Connect. If the network is secured, you will be prompted to enter the network security key (Wi-Fi password).

      Step 4

      Verify that the Wi-Fi connection is active by checking that the connected network icon appears in the system tray (Wi-Fi status icon showing an active connection).

      System Updates

      Before proceeding with any further configuration or optimization, it is essential to update your operating system to the latest available build. Performing these updates ensures that your system is protected with the latest security patches, bug fixes, and stability improvements provided by Microsoft. We strongly advise completing this process before starting any other modifications to your machine.

      To perform the update correctly, please select the button below that matches your operating system (Windows 10 or Windows 11) to view the relevant instructions.

      Step 1

      Open the Start menu and click on the Settings icon (the gear symbol) to open the Windows configuration panel.

      Step 2

      In the main Settings menu, locate and click on Update & Security. This section is where you will manage all system-related updates and recovery options.

      Step 3

      Select Windows Update from the left-hand sidebar and click the Check for updates button. The system will scan for all available security and quality fixes. Install all identified updates and restart your computer when prompted. If the system detects further updates after a restart, repeat this process until the message indicates that your device is fully up to date.

      Avoid OS Upgrades If you are running Windows 10, Windows Update may offer you an upgrade to Windows 11. Do not accept this upgrade during the update process. Our current objective is to secure and optimize your existing installation, not to perform a major OS version upgrade.

      Step 1

      Open the Start menu and select the Settings app (usually represented by a gear icon) to access the system configuration panel.

      Step 2

      From the main Settings dashboard, locate and click on Windows Update in the left-hand sidebar.

      Step 3

      Click the Check for updates button. The system will scan for all available security and quality fixes. If updates are found, click Download & install. If the system is waiting for a restart, you will see a Restart now button; ensure you save your work and click it to finalize the installation.

      Step 4

      Once the update process is complete, the status should indicate "You're up to date." Your system is now fully patched and ready for further optimizations.

      Important If you see a notification or an option to "Download & install" a "Preview Update" (as shown in the screenshot), do not install it. Preview updates are pre-release builds meant for testing purposes and may contain unresolved bugs or compatibility issues. For maximum system stability and to ensure our optimization procedures perform as expected, strictly ignore these preview packages and only install verified, stable security.
      Last modified: July 3, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Microsoft Account

      This section covers Microsoft Account configuration. While a Microsoft Account is not required to use Windows, configuring one during the initial setup process enables access to Microsoft services such as OneDrive, Microsoft Store, settings synchronization, device management, and cloud backup features. Linking a local user profile to a Microsoft Account is entirely optional, and users may continue using a local account if preferred. However, completing this configuration during the initial setup phase can simplify access to Microsoft ecosystem features and ensure that account-related services are available immediately after installation. If you do not wish to sign in with a Microsoft Account, you may skip this step and continue to the next section. A Microsoft Account can be linked to the device at any time later without affecting core operating system functionality.

      Step 1

      Open the Settings menu and navigate to the Accounts section. In the "Microsoft account" card, click the Sign in button. This initiates the connection process between your OS and Microsoft services.

      Step 2

      A secure authentication window will appear. Enter your Microsoft account credentials (email, phone number, or Skype ID) into the field and click Next to proceed. Once authenticated, your system will finalize the link between your local profile and your Microsoft identity.

      Last modified: July 15, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Account Security

      Securing your user profile is a standard practice to prevent unauthorized access to your local data. Whether you need to set a new password or change an existing one, Windows provides a centralized interface to manage all authentication methods, including PINs, security keys, and traditional passwords.

      Credential Responsibility We assume no responsibility for forgotten passwords, account lockouts, or any issues arising from lost credentials. You are solely responsible for keeping your password safe and ensuring you have a method to recover or remember your access key. Please store your credentials securely; if you lose access to your account due to a forgotten password, you may be unable to recover your local data.

      Follow these steps to configure your security credentials:

      Step 1

      Open the Settings menu and navigate to Accounts. From here, select Sign-in options. This menu displays all the methods available to authenticate your session, such as Windows Hello or standard passwords.

      Step 2

      Locate the Password section and click the Add button. This will open the password creation dialog.

      Step 3

      In the "Create a password" window, enter your desired password in both the "New password" and "Confirm password" fields. You may also add a "Password hint" to help you recall your credentials if forgotten. Click Next to finalize the setup.

      Last modified: July 8, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Windows Activation

      Verifying that your operating system is properly activated is a fundamental step. A valid activation ensures that your Windows license is recognized by Microsoft’s servers, allowing the system to operate with full functionality, receive all critical security updates, and unlock personalization settings.

      Follow these steps to verify your activation status:

      Step 1

      Open the Settings menu. In the left-hand sidebar, select System. Scroll down through the system options and locate and click on Activation to view your current license details.

      Step 2

      Check the Activation state. If it displays "Active" with a green checkmark, your system is correctly licensed and fully authorized. If your system shows as "Not active," ensure that you have a valid product key or a digital license linked to your account. You can click the Change button to input a product key or use the "Help with Activation" links provided on the page to troubleshoot authorization issues or verify your license availability.

      AMD Chipset Guide

      To begin, we will install the chipset drivers, which are essential software components that allow the operating system to properly communicate with the motherboard controller. In practice, they manage and optimize the operation of the main hardware interfaces, such as PCIe lanes, USB ports, and storage controllers.

      We start with these drivers because they form the foundation on which all the others rely: if the chipset is not correctly configured, even drivers such as those for the graphics card, network, or audio may not function properly or may become unstable. By installing them first, we ensure that the system is correctly recognized, stable, and ready for the subsequent drivers.

      Step 1

      Open any search engine and type "amd driver". Click on the first official AMD result: "Drivers and Support for Processors and Graphics".

      Step 2

      Scroll down the page to the "Search or Browse Drivers and Support by Product" section. Inside the "Browse Products" box, select "Chipsets". Refer to the image below for the exact configuration required in this step.

      Step 3

      In the "Product Family" section, select your motherboard's socket (in the photo example, "AM4"). If you do not know your exact hardware configuration, please consult your motherboard's official documentation or do a quick web search before proceeding.

      Step 4

      In the "Product Line" section, select the exact chipset model of your motherboard (in the photo example, "A520").

      Step 5

      Once you have confirmed that all selections match your hardware, click the "Submit" button to proceed. Refer to the image below for the exact configuration required in this step.

      Step 6

      Expand the section corresponding to your operating system (in the photo example, "Windows 11 - 64-Bit Edition"). Next, locate "AMD Chipset Drivers" and click the "Download" button to start the download.

      Step 7

      Wait for the download to complete successfully.

      Step 8

      Open File Explorer and navigate to the folder where the downloaded file was saved. Right-click the program file and select "Run as administrator".

      Step 9

      Wait for the program to complete the extraction of the necessary files for the installation. Do not close the window or interrupt the process during this phase.

      Step 10

      The AMD installation screen will appear. Click the "Accept & Express Install" button to proceed with the quick installation of the necessary drivers.

      Step 11

      Wait for the installation to complete. Do not turn off your computer or attempt to interrupt the process during this phase.

      Step 12

      The installation has been successfully completed. Click the "Close" button to exit the program. We recommend restarting your computer to ensure all drivers are properly loaded by the system. Refer to the image below for the exact configuration required in this step.

      Intel Chipset Guide

      To begin, we will install the chipset drivers, which are essential software components that allow the operating system to properly communicate with the motherboard controller. In practice, they manage and optimize the operation of the main hardware interfaces, such as PCIe lanes, USB ports, and storage controllers.

      We start with these drivers because they form the foundation on which all the others rely: if the chipset is not correctly configured, even drivers such as those for the graphics card, network, or audio may not function properly or may become unstable. By installing them first, we ensure that the system is correctly recognized, stable, and ready for the subsequent drivers.

      For chipset driver installation, we use Snappy Driver Installer Origin (SDIO). This tool automatically scans the system and identifies the most suitable drivers for the detected hardware.

      SDIO helps simplify the installation process, reducing the time required to manually search for drivers from different manufacturers. It also minimizes compatibility issues by recommending the correct driver versions for the system.

      Step 1

      Open any search engine and search for "snappy driver origin".

      Step 2

      Click on the link pointing to "Glenn's Page" to access the official website for Snappy Driver Installer Origin. Avoid clicking on sponsored results or other unofficial sites.

      Step 3

      Scroll down to the "Downloads" section and click on the first link, "Snappy Driver Installer Origin Version 1.18.0" (or the latest version available), to start downloading the application's .zip file.

      Step 4

      Wait for the download to complete successfully.

      Step 5

      Open File Explorer and navigate to your downloads folder. Right-click on the compressed zip file and select "Extract All..." from the context menu.

      Step 6

      In the extraction window, leave the default destination path unchanged. Ensure that the "Show extracted files when complete" checkbox is checked, and then click the "Extract" button in the bottom-right corner to proceed.

      Step 7

      Once the extraction is complete, the folder containing the program files will open. Right-click on the 64-bit executable (identified by the _x64 suffix within the filename, matching your system platform) and select the "Run as administrator" option to launch it.

      Step 8

      When you launch the program for the first time, a license agreement window (GNU General Public License) will appear. Click the "Accept" button in the bottom-right corner to agree to the terms and access the main interface.

      Step 9

      In case a Windows Defender Firewall security alert appears, simply click the "Allow access" button.

      Step 10

      On the welcome screen, click the third and last button labeled "Download Indexes Only". This will quickly scan your PC to identify missing or outdated drivers without downloading the entire driver package database.

      Step 11

      Wait for the index download to complete. The progress bar at the top displays the real-time download status; do not close the program or disconnect your internet connection during this phase.

      Step 12

      Once the index download is complete, locate the left sidebar and check the box labeled "Expert mode". This will unlock the advanced options and filters of the program, giving you more precise control over the driver installation.

      Step 13

      Verify that only the exact options shown in the screenshot are selected on the left menu: "Not installed", "Newer", "Better match", and "Show only best". Make sure no other options are checked—not one more, and not one less—to ensure a precise configuration.

      Step 14

      IMPORTANT: Manually select the main (top-level) driver entries for your chipset, bus, or specific proprietary motherboard drivers that are not graphics drivers, like in my case Fujitsu. Make sure to only check the top-level (newest) options and avoid checking the nested alternatives listed underneath them. Do not select any display or graphics card drivers under any circumstances—such as "Intel(R) HD Graphics". Leave them unchecked to prevent driver conflicts, as graphics drivers must be installed separately and cleanly using the dedicated guides in this wiki.

      Step 15

      After carefully reviewing and verifying your driver selections based on the previous step, click the "Install" button on the left sidebar. Wait patiently for the download and installation process to finish completely without touching or interrupting the program.

      Step 16

      Verify that the driver installation has completed successfully. Double-check that no display or graphics driver—such as "Intel(R) HD Graphics"—was installed; if a graphics driver was accidentally installed, consult the Clean Driver (DDU) guide above to clean it before proceeding. Finally, perform a system restart to correctly apply and load all the newly installed drivers.

      Windows Update Driver Control

      Before proceeding with the installation of your drivers, it is important to understand that Windows Update may automatically update system drivers. Windows Update can, in some cases, replace manually installed drivers with newer or older versions available in its database in order to ensure overall system compatibility and stability. Drivers provided by Windows are designed to work with most devices and to ensure that everything functions correctly, but they often include only the basic features without the advanced optimisations specific to the manufacturer. Drivers released directly by hardware manufacturers such as Intel, NVIDIA, AMD or Realtek may include improvements in performance, stability, latency, audio quality or additional features compared to generic Windows drivers. In some situations, Windows Update may overwrite these manufacturer drivers and replace them with generic or different versions, which can change the behaviour of the device or, in rare cases, affect performance or functionality. For this reason, some users prefer to manage drivers manually and prevent Windows Update from updating them automatically, in order to maintain full control over the installed driver versions on their system.

      This section presents two methods to control Windows Update driver installation. Choose the method that best fits your system configuration:

      Recommended Approach It is advisable to use both methods if you are using Windows 10 or Windows 11, especially if you have a Professional or Enterprise edition. Using both methods together provides the most comprehensive control over driver installation.
      Disclaimer Modifying system settings can be sensitive. We take no responsibility for any issues arising from incorrect modifications. Please follow the steps exactly as listed below.

      Method 1: Device Installation Settings (Available on All Windows Versions)

      Step 1

      Press Windows + R on your keyboard to open the Run dialog. Type sysdm.cpl and press Enter to open System Properties.

      Step 2

      Click the Hardware tab.

      Step 3

      Click Device Installation Settings.

      Step 4

      Select No, then click Save Changes to apply the settings correctly.

      Important These changes may take effect after the next Windows Update scan or system restart.

      Method 2: Local Group Policy Editor (Recommended for Pro/Enterprise)

      Step 1

      Press Windows + R on your keyboard to open the Run dialog. Type gpedit.msc and press Enter to launch the Local Group Policy Editor.

      Step 2

      In the left sidebar, navigate through the following path: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components.

      Step 3

      Locate the Windows Update folder in the list and select it, then open the Manage updates offered from Windows Update folder.

      Step 4

      In the right pane, locate the setting named "Do not include drivers with Windows Updates".

      Step 5

      Double-click on this policy. In the configuration window that opens, select the "Enabled" radio button, then click Apply and OK to save your changes.

      Important These changes may take effect after the next Windows Update scan or system restart.
      Need help? If you run into any issues or have questions regarding these settings, feel free to reach out to us on Discord for support!
      Last modified: July 3, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Clean Driver (DDU) Guide

      Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU) is a specialized utility designed to perform a thorough, "clean" removal of graphics drivers. When you uninstall drivers through the standard Windows Control Panel, remnants such as registry keys, temporary files, and service entries are often left behind. These leftovers can cause driver conflicts, stuttering, or performance regressions over time.

      By using DDU to completely wipe these artifacts, and combining this with the Windows Update driver control policy configured in the previous section, you ensure that your system remains a "clean slate." This allows you to install your manufacturer’s drivers without interference, ensuring the highest stability and best performance possible.

      Follow these steps to clean your system drivers:

      Step 1

      Open any search engine and type "DDU download".

      Step 2

      Click the first official result: https://www.guru3d.com/download/display-driver-uninstaller-download/

      Step 3

      Click one of the two "Download Mirror" buttons.

      Step 4

      Verify that the download completes successfully.

      Step 5

      Go to the folder where the file was downloaded, right-click the file, and select "Extract All".

      Step 6

      In the extraction window, leave the default destination path unchanged. Make sure the "Show extracted files when complete" box is checked, then click the "Extract" button at the bottom to proceed.

      Step 7

      Inside the extracted folder, you will find a 7-Zip self-extracting archive. Right-click it and select "Run as administrator".

      Step 8

      In the small window that appears, click "Extract" again. This will create the final folder containing the actual DDU program.

      Step 9

      Verify that a folder named "DDU (version name)" has been created.

      Step 10

      Open the Start menu, search for "cmd", right-click Command Prompt, and select "Run as administrator".

      Step 11

      Type the following command exactly and press Enter:

      shutdown /r /o /f /t 0

      This will force an immediate restart into the Advanced Startup Options menu.

      Step 12

      On the blue screen that appears, select "Troubleshoot".

      Step 13

      Click "Advanced options".

      Step 14

      Select "Startup Settings".

      Step 15

      Click "Restart" in the lower-right corner.

      Step 16

      The PC will restart. You will see a numbered list: press 4 or F4 on your keyboard to enable Safe Mode.

      Step 17

      Sign in with your password. You will notice a lower resolution, a black background, and the words "Safe Mode" in the corners of the screen.

      Step 18

      Go back to the Downloads folder, open the DDU folder, and run Display Driver Uninstaller.exe as administrator.

      Step 19

      Click "OK" on any pop-up windows.

      Step 20

      In the next pop-up window, select all required options exactly as shown (do not skip any). Even if you do not have certain hardware, no issues will occur. Then click "Close".

      Step 21

      Click "Select Device Type" and choose "GPU".

      Step 22

      Select your graphics card model. If you have multiple GPUs or are unsure, select "All GPUs".

      Step 23

      After confirming all selections, click "Clean and restart".

      Step 24

      Wait for the cleanup process to complete. The screen may flicker during this process. Do not touch the PC. The system will restart automatically when finished.

      Important The system has completely removed all old graphics drivers from your PC. Follow the next steps to install the drivers cleanly and ensure maximum performance.

      Optimize Core Scheduling

      The Multimedia Class Scheduler Service governs how CPU resources are distributed between time-sensitive multimedia applications and standard background processes. By default, the system reserves a portion of CPU time for lower-priority tasks to prevent starvation. The proportion of CPU time reserved is dictated by a specific responsiveness metric. Lowering this metric to its absolute minimum valid threshold of ten percent ensures that foreground gaming and audio threads receive ninety percent of the processing power during their boosted phases. If this value is set to one hundred, the entire scheduling mechanism is disabled, which is detrimental to performance. The scheduling cycle itself is divided into a boosted duration and an exhausted duration. The total length of this cycle is controlled by the scheduler period. Reducing this period to its minimum floor of fifty thousand microseconds (five milliseconds) forces the CPU to evaluate and switch thread priorities much faster. Using the mathematical formula extracted from the documentation, a fifty thousand microsecond period combined with a ten percent responsiveness metric results in a boosted phase of forty-five thousand microseconds and a brief exhausted phase of only five thousand microseconds. This rapid cycling drastically reduces input delay.

      Network packet processing introduces another layer of latency. The Windows network driver stack frequently uses Deferred Procedure Calls (DPCs) to handle network card interrupts. Because these DPCs run at a higher interrupt request level than user-mode code, they can interrupt and delay time-sensitive media and gaming threads. To mitigate this, the scheduler utilizes a network throttling index. Setting this index to its maximum hexadecimal limit of 0xFFFFFFFF completely disables the NDIS throttle mechanism, ensuring that network throughput is not artificially restricted during gameplay or audio playback. Furthermore, the scheduler possesses an idle detection mechanism known as lazy mode. When the system detects CPU starvation over a set number of detection cycles, it forces threads into extended sleep states. By explicitly disabling this lazy mode, the scheduler is forced to strictly adhere to the aggressive boosted and exhausted cycles without ever dropping into deep sleep states. Thread capacity is also a critical factor. The scheduler enforces strict limits on the number of threads that can register for prioritized access. If an application spawns too many threads, it will encounter a "STATUS_TOO_MANY_THREADS" error. Expanding the maximum threads per process to one hundred twenty-eight and the total system-wide threads to sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-five guarantees that modern, highly multi-threaded game engines will never hit an artificial ceiling.

      Visual evidence from the provided Windows Performance Analyzer (WPA) and WinDbg captures corroborates these internal mechanics. WinDbg traces reveal the core scheduler thread operating at a base priority of twenty-seven and a priority floor of twenty-seven, with an I/O priority of two and a page priority of five. The thread wait start tick count is logged at 224914, with a context switch count of 376449 on ideal processor two. WPA graphs visually demonstrate the split between boosted and exhausted phases, displaying distinct blocks labeled 10 (0xA) and 100 (0x64). Further WPA captures detail the exact sleep durations, showing DeepSleep states lasting 4,294,967,295 units, SleepRealtimeLazy at 2,000,000 units, Realtime at 35,000 units, and SleepResponsiveness at 15,000 units. Another capture highlights the idle detection cycle triggering exactly twenty-one times before hitting the threshold of twenty-two. By disabling lazy mode and tightening the scheduler period, these extended sleep states are entirely bypassed in favor of continuous, high-frequency execution.

      RISKS

      No significant risks for gaming scenarios or context.

      BENEFITS

      This optimization delivers the absolute highest CPU prioritization for gaming and audio workloads. It eliminates network throttling to stabilize ping, prevents the CPU from entering lazy sleep states, and dramatically increases the frequency of thread scheduling. The result is a highly responsive system with perfectly stable frame times and zero audio crackling under heavy load.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "SystemResponsiveness" /t REG_DWORD /d 10 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "NetworkThrottlingIndex" /t REG_DWORD /d 4294967295 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "NoLazyMode" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "IdleDetectionCycles" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "LazyModeTimeout" /t REG_DWORD /d 1000000 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "SchedulerTimerResolution" /t REG_DWORD /d 10000 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "SchedulerPeriod" /t REG_DWORD /d 50000 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "MaxThreadsPerProcess" /t REG_DWORD /d 128 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Multimedia\SystemProfile" /v "MaxThreadsTotal" /t REG_DWORD /d 65535 /f
echo Optimize MMCSS Core Scheduling and Thread Limits for SystemProfile applied successfully.
pause

      Optimize Task Profiles

      Applications must manually register with the Multimedia Class Scheduler Service by calling specific API functions, informing the system of the exact task they are performing. Once registered, the scheduler uses registry-defined task profiles to determine the relative priority of those threads. The most critical parameter within these profiles is the scheduling category. Assigning a task to the "High" category forces its base thread priority to twenty-four, which is higher than almost all standard system-level tasks. From this base of twenty-four, the relative priority parameter can push the final boosted priority even higher, allowing it to fluctuate between twenty-three and twenty-six. By setting the relative priority to its maximum value of eight, we guarantee that the thread receives the absolute highest tier of execution precedence within its category. Furthermore, the scheduler supports a parameter that dictates the priority of a thread when it voluntarily yields its execution time. Setting this yield priority to its maximum limit of nineteen ensures that even when a game engine briefly pauses to wait for data, it does not fall into a heavily degraded priority state.

      Several other parameters exist within these task profiles to fine-tune resource allocation. The clock rate acts as a hint for the granularity of processor resource scheduling. While its strict enforcement was altered in newer Windows versions to save power, explicitly defining it to the maximum value of ten thousand guarantees no legacy latency penalties are applied. It is also imperative to explicitly declare that these tasks are not background processes. Setting the background flag to false ensures that the threads are immune to priority degradation caused by changes in window focus. Although the documentation notes that parameters such as GPU Priority, SFIO Priority, and Latency Sensitive flags are either unused by the driver or have no observable effect, explicitly defining them to their maximum theoretical states (such as setting SFIO Priority to High and Latency Sensitive to True) ensures absolute coverage of all potential scheduling edge cases without causing harm. Processor affinity is left at zero, which acts as a bitmask instructing the scheduler to utilize all available logical processors without artificial restriction.

      Windows Performance Analyzer captures provided in the documentation visually confirm the impact of these task profiles. Traces reveal processes such as `audiodg.exe` (PID 5608) and `Spotify.exe` (PID 10772) actively calling `Thread_SetChars` and `Thread_Join` to bind themselves to the Audio task. The resulting graph plots show these threads executing at extreme priority levels of twenty-four, twenty-five, twenty-six, and twenty-seven. Another capture focusing on the `mmcss_task.exe` test tool (PID 10464 and PID 3796) perfectly illustrates the priority clamping behavior, showing that when the High category is utilized, the threads are strictly bound to the upper echelons of the Windows priority matrix, completely preempting standard user-mode applications.

      RISKS

      No significant risks for gaming scenarios or context.

      BENEFITS

      By forcing Games, Audio, and Window Manager tasks into the "High" scheduling category with maximum relative priority, the operating system is forced to process rendering and input threads before anything else. This completely eliminates micro-stutters caused by background tasks stealing CPU cycles and ensures perfectly synchronized audio playback.

      Optimize Kernel Timer Scheduling

      The Windows kernel must determine the most optimal processor to handle timer expirations when a timer is inserted. By default on modern client systems, especially those supporting Modern Standby, the kernel enforces timer serialization. This mechanism forces all kernel timers (KTIMER) to be queued and processed exclusively on the timer table of CPU 0, making it the permanent clock owner. While this allows other processors to enter deep sleep states for power efficiency, it creates a significant asynchronous bottleneck on CPU 0 during high-performance workloads like gaming. By modifying the `SerializeTimerExpiration` registry value in the Session Manager Kernel configuration and setting it to a value of two, this serialization is forcibly disabled. Disabling serialization instructs the kernel to use the individual Processor Control Block (PRCB) timer table for the current processor. As visually demonstrated in the provided timer queuing diagrams and WinDbg `!timer` dumps, this shifts the behavior from funneling all timers into CPU 0 to distributing them evenly across the active processors, drastically reducing the processing burden on a single core.

      In conjunction with timer distribution, the `EnablePerCpuClockTickScheduling` parameter dictates whether clock tick scheduling relies on a global clock state or a localized per-PRCB state. Setting this value to one ensures that each processor maintains its own independent timer state variables, such as the next tick due time and the requested time increment, rather than synchronizing with a global value. Furthermore, the system's dynamic tick feature allows the kernel to suppress periodic clock ticks when processors transition into idle states, invoking routines like `KePrepareClockTimerForIdle`. Visual traces from Windows Performance Analyzer and debugger outputs confirm that disabling dynamic tick prevents the system from skipping these periodic ticks. When dynamic tick is disabled, the kernel bypasses the idle preparation phase, ensuring that the clock owner maintains a continuous and highly accurate timer resolution without the latency overhead of waking up and recalculating the next tick due time.

      RISKS

      Disabling timer serialization and dynamic tick will prevent the system from entering deep power-saving states and breaks Modern Standby resiliency phases. This will lead to higher baseline power consumption and increased heat generation, which is generally only a concern for battery-powered portable devices.

      BENEFITS

      Distributing timers across all processors eliminates the CPU 0 bottleneck, which is critical for heavily multi-threaded game engines and high-polling-rate peripherals. Disabling dynamic tick and enabling per-CPU scheduling ensures the lowest possible timer latency, perfectly consistent tick intervals, and a reduction in cross-processor synchronization overhead, leading to smoother frame times and reduced input delay.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "SerializeTimerExpiration" /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "EnablePerCpuClockTickScheduling" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
bcdedit /set disabledynamictick yes
echo Disable Timer Serialization and Optimize Clock Tick Scheduling applied successfully.
pause

      Revert Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
reg delete "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "SerializeTimerExpiration" /f
reg delete "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "EnablePerCpuClockTickScheduling" /f
bcdedit /deletevalue disabledynamictick
echo Restore Timer Serialization and Optimize Clock Tick Scheduling applied successfully.
pause
      Last modified: July 9, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Optimize Priority Separation

      Windows utilizes a quantum-based preemptive scheduler to distribute processor time among active threads. A quantum represents the maximum amount of time a thread is permitted to execute before the kernel pauses it to evaluate if another thread of equal or higher priority requires the CPU. This thread run-time accounting is not measured in simple clock ticks, but rather in processor cycles, known as Quantum Units. The core mechanism governing how these quantums are distributed between foreground and background processes is controlled by a six-bit registry value called Win32PrioritySeparation. This value is divided into three distinct two-bit pairs. The lowest bits, zero and one, dictate the foreground priority boost multiplier. Setting these bits to a binary value of one-zero applies a maximum plus-two priority boost, mathematically ensuring that the foreground process receives three times the processor time compared to background processes.

      The middle bits, two and three, determine whether the quantum allocation is variable or fixed. When configured as variable, the scheduler uses a dynamic table where background processes receive a base allocation of six Quantum Units, while the boosted foreground process receives a massive eighteen Quantum Units. If a fixed table were used instead, all processes would receive an identical eighteen Quantum Units regardless of their foreground status, completely neutralizing the intended priority boost. The highest bits, four and five, control the base length of the clock interval. Setting these bits to a binary value of one-zero forces a short interval. Short intervals trigger more frequent scheduler evaluations, which is absolutely critical for client systems and gaming environments because it drastically minimizes input latency and ensures rapid context switching when user input is detected. Combining these optimal binary pairs results in a final binary string of one-zero-zero-one-one-zero, which translates to a decimal value of thirty-eight or a hexadecimal value of 0x26. Enforcing this specific value guarantees the maximum theoretical processor time ratio in favor of the active game.

      To complement the quantum allocation, the kernel also manages how long a dynamic priority boost lasts via the ForceForegroundBoostDecay policy located in the Session Manager. By default, Windows is designed to maintain the foreground boost as long as the process remains active on the screen. However, explicitly defining this value to zero forcefully prevents the scheduler functions, such as KiQuantumEnd, from decaying or stripping away the priority boost over time. Visual evidence from the provided Windows Performance Recorder captures perfectly illustrates this behavior. When the separation is active, the thread priority dynamically boosts, forming a distinct oscillating waveform between priority eight and ten. Furthermore, the documentation highlights a critical anomaly in Windows 11 version 23H2, where having the native Game Mode enabled inadvertently breaks this foreground priority boost, resulting in a flat, unboosted priority line in Performance Monitor. While this scheduling bug appears resolved in version 25H2, explicitly locking the Win32PrioritySeparation and ForceForegroundBoostDecay values ensures the deepest level of scheduler compliance possible. Debugger outputs further confirm these mechanics, showing the exact hexadecimal values of the variable quantum tables and verifying the processor cycle calculations against an AMD processor running at 3700 megahertz.

      RISKS

      No significant risks for gaming scenarios or context. Background applications (such as file downloads, video rendering, or heavy browser tabs) will receive significantly less CPU time and may execute slower while a demanding game is running in the foreground.

      BENEFITS

      This optimization guarantees that the active foreground game receives absolute priority over background system tasks. By enforcing short, variable quantums with a maximum 3x time multiplier, input latency is minimized, and frame times are stabilized. Preventing priority decay ensures that this performance state does not degrade during long gaming sessions.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\PriorityControl" /v "Win32PrioritySeparation" /t REG_DWORD /d 38 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "ForceForegroundBoostDecay" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
echo Optimize Win32PrioritySeparation and Foreground Boost Decay applied successfully.
pause

      Revert Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\PriorityControl" /v "Win32PrioritySeparation" /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f
reg delete "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "ForceForegroundBoostDecay" /f
echo Restore Win32PrioritySeparation and Foreground Boost Decay applied successfully.
pause
      Last modified: July 12, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Optimize DWM GPU Scheduling

      The Desktop Window Manager is the Windows subsystem responsible for compositing visible window rendering into a single surface. By default, it collects offscreen buffers from various applications and combines them into a final desktop image. This composition process introduces latency and overhead. To maximize gaming performance, this optimization forces the system to bypass traditional composition in favor of direct scanout methods like Multiplane Overlay and Independent Flip. By setting the overlay minimum frame rate to zero and forcing the overlay test mode to four, the graphics kernel is instructed to aggressively assign swap chains to dedicated hardware overlay planes regardless of the application's frame rate. This ensures that games and hardware-accelerated applications communicate directly with the display hardware, eliminating the intermediate copy to the compositor backbuffer.

      Furthermore, all unnecessary visual enhancements managed by the compositor are strictly disabled. Features such as projected shadows, window animations, backdrop blur caching, and colorization are turned off to free up GPU cycles and memory bandwidth. The configuration also disables device bitmaps and hologram compositing to reduce memory locking and background driver polling. Telemetry reporting intervals and animation attribution hashing are completely neutralized to prevent background CPU spikes during rendering workloads. Finally, the system is instructed to always use the fastest monitor as the primary display, ensuring that the highest refresh rate panel receives priority synchronization, while mouse wheel and mode change animations are reduced to zero milliseconds for instantaneous responsiveness.

      RISKS

      Disabling Desktop Window Manager animations and shadows will result in a visually rigid desktop experience. Forcing Multiplane Overlays can cause flickering or black screens on systems with unstable GPU drivers. Disabling device bitmaps may cause minor visual artifacts in legacy applications that rely on older rendering APIs.

      BENEFITS

      Significantly reduces input lag and frame presentation latency by bypassing the Windows compositor. Eliminates micro-stutters caused by background telemetry and visual effect rendering. Maximizes the probability that a game will run in Independent Flip mode, granting it exclusive control over the display's presentation queue.
