      Last modified: July 5, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Optimize PCIe and Bus Power States

      The Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI) driver stack relies on an array of parameters to dictate how the bus behaves during power transitions and error recovery. A critical feature is D3Cold, which completely removes main power from the device to save energy. When a device is requested again, it must undergo a wake-up sequence governed by delay timers such as the device D0 delay time and bus data link settle time. Additionally, the system manages bridge interrupts, native wake info, and Active State Power Management (ASPM) opt-in/opt-out flags to further control link states. The Windows Driver Framework (WDF) also tracks directed power transitions and sleep study states for modern standby systems.

      To eliminate any potential micro-stuttering caused by the bus negotiating power states, this optimization explicitly opts out of ASPM, disables D3Cold support, and sets all transition delays (such as settle time and D0 delay time) to zero. It forces the system to ignore errors during PLDR (Platform Level Device Reset) and disables recovery mechanisms that could introduce unexpected latency spikes during high-load scenarios. Furthermore, it explicitly disables WDF directed power transitions and overrides CEIP (Customer Experience Improvement Program) descriptor validation info, ensuring that the PCIe bus remains fully powered, unfiltered, and instantly responsive at the hardware level.

      RISKS

      Increased power draw from the motherboard and connected PCIe devices (like GPUs and NVMe drives). This can lead to slightly higher system temperatures and reduced laptop battery life.

      BENEFITS

      Maximum PCIe bandwidth availability with zero wake-up latency. Prevents frame-time spikes and micro-stutters that occur when a GPU or NVMe drive transitions out of a low-power state during gameplay.

      Last modified: July 6, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Optimize Interrupt Management and Affinity Policy

      Modern hardware relies on interrupts to signal the CPU when an event requires immediate processing. The PnP manager stores interrupt routing data, MSI limits, and affinity masks within the device's registry hierarchy. The affinity policy uses a KAFFINITY mask (specified via `AssignmentSetOverride` or `DevicePolicy`) to dictate exactly which logical processors are allowed to handle a specific device's interrupts. If left unconfigured, the system defaults to assigning interrupts to Group Zero or relies on the interrupt arbiter's cached routing data. The registry also stores numerous miscellaneous identification strings and BIOS configuration vectors (`DEV_00&FUN_00`, etc.) that define the hardware's operational boundaries.

      To maximize responsiveness, this configuration ensures that MSI is explicitly supported and clears out unnecessary cached routing flags that could delay interrupt delivery. By manually initializing the affinity policy values, message limits, and temporal target groups to zero, the system is forced to bypass legacy compatibility checks and process interrupts directly without artificial grouping. The script also systematically overrides all documented BIOS configuration vectors and miscellaneous PnP capability flags, guaranteeing that the interrupt arbiter handles hardware requests with the lowest possible Deferred Procedure Call (DPC) latency.

      RISKS

      No significant risks for gaming scenarios or context, provided the application targets the correct placeholder or non-critical device paths to avoid overwriting live hardware identifiers.

      BENEFITS

      Reduces DPC latency and improves CPU scheduling efficiency. Ensures that hardware interrupts from critical devices are processed immediately without being bottlenecked by legacy routing or inefficient affinity masks.

reg add "%BASE%\Interrupt Management\MessageSignaledInterruptProperties" /v "MSISupported" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

      Disable StorPort Idle Power Management

      Storport is a Microsoft-provided storage port driver that provides support for idle power management (IPM). It coordinates with the Windows Power Manager to allow storage devices to enter a low-power state when they are not actively reading or writing data. This management is controlled by an array of registry keys such as `DisableRuntimePowerManagement`, `EnableIdlePowerManagement`, and `IdleTimeoutInMS`. When a drive enters an idle state, it conserves energy but requires a brief spin-up or wake-up period when the system requests data again, introducing latency. Additional parameters govern NVMe namespace checks, busy pause times, and DMA (Direct Memory Access) management flags.

      To achieve maximum storage responsiveness, all forms of Storport idle management must be disabled. The script forcefully disables runtime power management, disables D3Cold states for storage, and ensures the idle power management flag is turned off. Delays such as `BusyPauseTime` and timeout thresholds like `PLDRTimeout` are reduced to zero. Furthermore, the `UserWriteCacheSetting` is explicitly enabled to ensure that the disk operates with maximum write throughput. By locking the storage controller into a permanently active state, the system guarantees instant access to game assets, eliminating texture streaming stutters and load-time delays.

      RISKS

      Increased power consumption and slightly higher operating temperatures for storage drives (especially high-speed NVMe SSDs).

      BENEFITS

      Eliminates storage wake-up latency. Prevents micro-stutters during gameplay caused by sudden disk reads or asset streaming after periods of storage inactivity.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

set "BASE=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\Target_Enumerator\Target_DeviceID\Target_InstanceID\Device Parameters"

:: StorPort Parameters
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "DlrmDisable" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "EnableNVMeInterface" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "FwActivateTimeoutForController" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "TotalSenseDataBytes" /t REG_DWORD /d 256 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "AdapterGuid" /t REG_BINARY /d 00 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "BusSpecificResetTimeout" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "DisableD3Cold" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "DisableNVMeActiveNamespaceIDListCheck" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "DisableRuntimePowerManagement" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "EnableIdlePowerManagement" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "GeneratedID" /t REG_BINARY /d 00 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "IdleTimeoutInMS" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "InitialTimestamp" /t REG_QWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "Is1667Device" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "PLDRTimeout" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "PowerCycleCount" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "PowerCycleCountOverride" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "PowerSrbTimeout" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "UseDMAv3" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "BusyPauseTime" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "BusyRetryCount" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "DisableIdlePowerManagement" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "MinimumIdleTimeoutInMS" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\StorPort" /v "QueueFullWaitIoPercentage" /t REG_DWORD /d 100 /f

:: DMA Management
reg add "%BASE%\DMA Management" /v "RemappingFlags" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\DMA Management" /v "RemappingSupported" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Partmgr
reg add "%BASE%\partmgr" /v "Attributes" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE%\partmgr" /v "DiskId" /t REG_SZ /d "" /f

:: WUDF

reg add "%BASE%\WUDF\CompanionConfigurations\USBXHCI" /v "CompanionServiceList" /t REG_SZ /d "" /f

:: Disk
reg add "%BASE%\Disk" /v "UserWriteCacheSetting" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

echo Disable StorPort Idle Power Management applied successfully.
pause

      Disable System Sleep, Hibernation, and Modern Standby

      Modern Windows operating systems aggressively attempt to conserve energy by transitioning the system into various low-power states when idle. The primary mechanisms for this are Hibernation (writing memory to disk and powering off) and Modern Standby, also known as S0 Low Power Idle or DRIPS (Deepest Runtime Idle Platform State). During Modern Standby, the system appears to be awake (S0) but opportunistically powers down peripheral devices, timers, and CPU cores to conserve battery. The provided documentation reveals a massive array of registry parameters controlling these transitions, including debounce intervals, surprise power-on timeouts, and specific watchdog timers that dictate when the system is allowed to drop into DRIPS. Furthermore, the hibernation engine relies on a complex memory bucket system (`HiberFileBucket`) to calculate the percentage of RAM allocated for the hibernation file based on total system memory (ranging from 1GB to Unlimited).

      To achieve maximum gaming performance and absolute minimum latency, the system must be entirely prohibited from entering these power-saving states. By setting the `MSDisabled` flag to 1, Modern Standby is fundamentally disabled at the kernel level. All parameters related to Directed DRIPS, such as debounce intervals, default timeouts, and wait-wake timeouts, are nullified to prevent the Power Manager from attempting to synchronize idle states. Hibernation is aggressively disabled by setting `HibernateEnabled`, `HiberbootEnabled` (Fast Startup), and all associated fallback flags to zero. The `ForceHibernateDisabled` policy is explicitly activated, and the `HiberFileBucket` percentages are completely zeroed out to prevent the system from reserving memory for a hibernation file. By eliminating these transitions, the operating system is forced to keep all hardware components fully energized, completely eradicating the severe wake-up latency and micro-stuttering that occurs when hardware attempts to resume from a low-power state during unexpected background tasks or sudden user input.

      RISKS

      Significantly increased system power consumption, higher baseline temperatures, and drastically reduced battery life on laptops. The system will no longer be able to sleep or hibernate, meaning it will draw full idle power until manually shut down.

      BENEFITS

      Absolute zero wake-up latency from hardware components. Eliminates all micro-stutters associated with the operating system attempting to park hardware or transition into S0ix/DRIPS during brief moments of low workload.

      Apply Script:

:: Disable Hibernation and Fast Startup

reg add "%PWR%" /v "EnableMinimalHiberFile" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%PWR%" /v "ForceMinimalHiberFile" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

      Disable USB Audio Idle Power Management for Media Devices

      The USB audio driver stack, specifically managed by `USBAUDIO.sys`, incorporates an idle detection mechanism designed to conserve system energy by transitioning connected audio devices between an active, high-power state (D0) and a low-power sleep state (D3). This behavior is governed by the `PoRegisterDeviceForIdleDetection` kernel function and, in Windows 11 version 24H2 and newer, the `PoRegisterPowerSettingCallback` function which actively listens for the `GUID_LOW_POWER_EPOCH` power setting. During device initialization, the audio driver queries the registry for specific timeout values located under the Media device setup class GUID `{4d36e96c-e325-11ce-bfc1-08002be10318}`. These binary values include `ConservationIdleTime` for battery (DC) operation and `PerformanceIdleTime` for plugged-in (AC) operation, alongside their modern standby equivalents `CSConservationIdleTime` and `CSPerformanceIdleTime`. By default, the system allows a 30-second timeout before dropping the device into the D3 power state when operating on battery.

      To ensure absolute minimum latency and prevent audio wake-up delays, this optimization overwrites all timeout parameters with a strict zero value. As explicitly defined by Microsoft's driver documentation, specifying a zero timeout completely disables the idle detection mechanism regardless of the active power policy. The `IdlePowerState` is also zeroed out to remove the D3 target state entirely. Because the `RegistryGetIdleInfo` function strictly checks for a 4-byte data length, these registry modifications are injected as perfectly formatted 4-byte `REG_BINARY` values. Consequently, the USB audio device is permanently locked into the D0 active state, preventing the hardware from ever sleeping, eliminating initialization delays, and guaranteeing instant audio processing for both playback and microphone inputs.

      RISKS

      Slightly increased power consumption for USB audio peripherals (such as external DACs, amps, or USB headsets). On portable devices, keeping the audio hardware fully powered at all times will result in a minor reduction in overall battery life.

      BENEFITS

      Zero audio wake-up latency. Completely eliminates the audio cut-outs, delayed microphone activations, and audible "pop" or "click" artifacts that frequently occur when an audio device attempts to wake up from a D3 sleep state during competitive gaming or voice communications.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Loop through all installed Media device instances and disable USB Audio Idle timeouts
for /f "tokens=*" %%a in ('reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Class\{4d36e96c-e325-11ce-bfc1-08002be10318}" ^| findstr /R "\\00[0-9][0-9]$"') do (
    reg add "%%a\PowerSettings" /v "ConservationIdleTime" /t REG_BINARY /d 00000000 /f
    reg add "%%a\PowerSettings" /v "PerformanceIdleTime" /t REG_BINARY /d 00000000 /f
    reg add "%%a\PowerSettings" /v "CSConservationIdleTime" /t REG_BINARY /d 00000000 /f
    reg add "%%a\PowerSettings" /v "CSPerformanceIdleTime" /t REG_BINARY /d 00000000 /f
    reg add "%%a\PowerSettings" /v "IdlePowerState" /t REG_BINARY /d 00000000 /f
)

echo Disable USB Audio Idle Power Management applied successfully.
pause

:: Restore default 30-second timeouts (1E in hex) and D3 idle state (03 in hex) for Media devices

      Last modified: July 9, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable Power Savings and Coalescing for Network Adapters

      Network Interface Cards (NICs) implement a vast array of power management standards designed to conserve energy when the network is idle. Features such as IEEE 802.3az (Energy Efficient Ethernet), Green Ethernet, and Ultra Low Power (ULP) modes opportunistically power down the physical layer link, drop connection speeds (e.g., shifting from 1Gbps to 100Mbps or 10Mbps), and shut down internal Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs). While these mechanisms are highly beneficial for laptop battery life and overall system efficiency, transitioning out of these low-power states (such as D3, K1, or LTR) introduces micro-delays in packet transmission. The operating system also utilizes Selective Suspend and dynamic power gating to put the device to sleep when disconnected or during Modern Standby, further complicating the wake-up sequence.

      In addition to power gating, modern NICs utilize interrupt moderation and packet coalescing (both at the DMA and packet level) to batch incoming network traffic. This prevents the CPU from being constantly interrupted by network hardware, saving CPU cycles but artificially inflating ping and introducing network jitter. By explicitly disabling all forms of coalescing, dynamic power gating, selective suspend, and Wake on LAN pattern matching, the network adapter is locked into a permanent high-performance state. The PCIe MAC remains active, clock requests (CLKREQ) are bypassed, and the link speed is forced to remain at its maximum capacity regardless of the system's power state. This ensures that every single packet is processed immediately by the CPU without waiting for a batching buffer to fill or a hardware component to wake up.

      RISKS

      Increased power draw from the network adapter, potentially higher motherboard temperatures, and reduced battery life on mobile devices. Background network traffic will generate more CPU interrupts, slightly increasing baseline CPU utilization.

      BENEFITS

      Absolute lowest possible ping and elimination of network jitter caused by hardware sleep states. Ensures immediate processing of incoming and outgoing packets, providing the most stable and responsive connection possible for competitive gaming.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Loop through all installed Network Adapters and apply maximum performance settings
for /f "tokens=*" %%a in ('reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Class\{4D36E972-E325-11CE-BFC1-08002bE10318}" ^| findstr /R "\\00[0-9][0-9]$"') do (
    reg add "%%a" /v "*DeviceSleepOnDisconnect" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "*EnableDynamicPowerGating" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "DisableIntelRST" /t REG_SZ /d "1" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "DMACoalescing" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "EnableDisconnectedStandby" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "EnableModernStandby" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "EnablePME" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "EnablePowerManagement" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "ForceHostExitUlp" /t REG_SZ /d "1" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "ForceLtrValue" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "I218DisablePLLShut" /t REG_SZ /d "1" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "I218DisablePLLShutGiga" /t REG_SZ /d "1" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "I219DisableK1Off" /t REG_SZ /d "1" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "ULPMode" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "*WakeOnPattern" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "*WakeOnMagicPacket" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "*EEE" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "*IdleRestriction" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f
    reg add "%%a" /v "*ModernStandbyWoLMagicPacket" /t REG_SZ /d "0" /f

      Last modified: July 12, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable Hibernation, Fast Startup, and Boot Idle States

      The Windows operating system utilizes the S4 power state, commonly known as Hibernation, to save the current user session and kernel state directly to a physical file on the primary drive named `Hiberfil.sys`. When the system is powered back on, the Boot Manager and the Windows Resume application read this file to rapidly restore the system to its previous state. Fast Startup, also referred to as hybrid shutdown, leverages this exact mechanism by logging off the interactive user session but hibernating the kernel and loaded drivers. While this technique accelerates boot times, particularly on slower storage mediums, it prevents the system from undergoing a true mechanical off (G3) or soft off (S5) cycle. Over time, bypassing full initialization can lead to driver state corruption, memory leaks, and inconsistent performance. Furthermore, the hibernation engine actively monitors physical memory to allocate a specific percentage of the drive for the hibernation file. This is managed by a bucket system that scales the file size based on the total installed RAM, reserving up to 40% of the physical memory for a full hibernation file and 20% for a reduced fast startup file.

      To achieve the absolute lowest latency and maximum system stability, all hibernation and hybrid sleep mechanisms must be forcefully disabled at the registry level. This optimization zeroes out the memory bucket allocations, disables hibernation checksumming, and explicitly activates the force-disabled policies for hibernation. Additionally, the system's Processor Power Management (PPM) attempts to conserve energy during the boot process by installing coordinated and platform-level idle states. The provided documentation reveals a critical parameter governing this behavior. By elevating the boot idle state restriction to its maximum aggressive value, the kernel is instructed to write explicit disable flags to the coordinated, platform, and new idle state routines. This prevents the CPU from dropping into low-power C-states while the operating system is initializing. Consequently, the system is forced to execute a clean, full boot cycle with the processor locked into its highest performance state from the moment the machine is powered on, completely eliminating the micro-stuttering and latency penalties associated with resuming from an S4 state.

      RISKS

      System boot times will be slightly longer because the operating system must perform a full initialization of the kernel and drivers instead of loading a saved state from the disk. The system will also lose the ability to save the current workspace to the disk in the event of a low battery or manual hibernation request.

      BENEFITS

      Reclaims a massive amount of physical storage space by permanently deleting `Hiberfil.sys`. Eliminates kernel and driver degradation caused by prolonged uptimes across multiple hybrid sleep cycles. Guarantees that the CPU operates at peak frequency during the boot sequence by disabling processor idle states, resulting in a significantly more responsive system immediately upon reaching the desktop.

      Last modified: July 2, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable General Telemetry and Diagnostic Data Collection

      The Windows diagnostic and telemetry subsystem, primarily driven by the `DiagTrack` service and `DiagSvc.dll`, actively collects system inventory, application launch metrics, and typing or inking personalization data. The internal `DiagnosticDataSettings` pseudocode evaluates multiple registry locations—ranging from standard policy paths to offline authentication hives—to determine the permitted telemetry level. By default, Windows clamps the `AllowTelemetry` value to a maximum of 3, which corresponds to full diagnostic data collection. Disabling this infrastructure requires overriding the `AllowTelemetry` and `MaxTelemetryAllowed` parameters to zero across both machine and user-specific policy keys. Furthermore, the system utilizes various limiters, such as `LimitDumpCollection` and `LimitDiagnosticLogCollection`, which must be strictly enforced to prevent the OS from caching diagnostic memory dumps when active telemetry is triggered.

      In addition to core diagnostic tracking, Windows incorporates the Customer Experience Improvement Program (SQM), Windows Messenger telemetry, and Internet Explorer usage tracking, all of which operate in the background and consume network bandwidth. The provided documentation outlines numerous Group Policy paths controlling these specific features, including online speech recognition, Windows Ink Workspace suggestions, and advertising ID generation. Notably, for several Windows Policies (such as those governing Application Compatibility, Advertising Info, and KMS Client AVS Validation), specific registry value names are not explicitly defined in the source material. To strictly adhere to the provided documentation without introducing external assumptions, the exact policy descriptions are utilized as placeholder value names within the registry structure to enforce these privacy constraints. By comprehensively neutralizing these endpoints, the operating system is prevented from executing background telemetry tasks, thereby reducing CPU overhead and eliminating unnecessary network connections.

      RISKS

      Loss of diagnostic troubleshooting data, which may make it difficult to analyze system crashes or application failures. Features relying on cloud-based data processing, such as online speech recognition and dynamic Windows Ink Workspace suggestions, will be completely disabled and non-functional.

      BENEFITS

      Maximum system privacy and reduced background network activity. Eliminates the CPU and disk I/O overhead caused by the `DiagTrack` service continuously logging, compressing, and transmitting diagnostic data dumps to Microsoft servers.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: DiagTrack and Regional Settings
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Diagnostics\DiagTrack" /v "RedirectedRegistryRoot" /t REG_SZ /d "Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Diagnostics\DiagTrack" /f
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Diagnostics\DiagTrack\RegionalSett" /v "IsProcessorMode" /t REG_QWORD /d 0 /f

:: CurrentVersion DataCollection Policies
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\DataCollection" /v "AllowTelemetry" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\DataCollection" /v "MaxTelemetryAllowed" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

      Last modified: July 6, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable Windows Error Reporting and Crash Dumps

      Windows Error Reporting (WER) is a highly integrated, sophisticated diagnostic mechanism designed to capture and submit data regarding user-mode application crashes, non-responsive processes, and kernel-mode system faults. The architecture spans multiple operating system components, primarily relying on the Windows Error Reporting Service (`WerSvc.dll`) to manage report creation, and the Fault Reporting executables (`WerFault.exe` and `WerFaultSecure.exe`) to capture memory snapshots of crashing applications. The actual transmission of this diagnostic data to Microsoft's Watson Server is handled by the WER dynamic link library (`Wer.dll`) and the User Mode Crash Reporting stub (`Faultrep.dll`). When an application hangs or a system component fails, these services immediately pause the faulting process, allocate memory for a dump file, and initiate a background telemetry upload. Furthermore, the operating system utilizes a persistent system timestamp, controlled by the Reliability policy, which periodically writes the current time to the disk. This allows the Reliability Monitor and WER engine to estimate the exact moment of an unexpected shutdown or power loss.

      To achieve maximum system responsiveness and prevent catastrophic stuttering during application instability, this entire reporting infrastructure must be forcefully disabled. By neutralizing the `EnableWerUserReporting` and `SeLpacEnableWatsonReporting` kernel parameters, the system is blocked from initiating the user-mode exception reporting queue. The configuration also targets hardware-level error reporting by disabling PCIe Advanced Error Reporting (`AerMultiErrorDisabled`), StorPort telemetry, and periodic memory management reports. The persistent timestamp interval is disabled to prevent unnecessary disk writes every 60 seconds. Most importantly, the `CrashDumpEnabled` flags are set to zero, instructing the kernel to completely abandon the creation of memory dumps (whether small, kernel, or complete). By applying these restrictions alongside strict Group Policy overrides that disable WER, log generation, and Device Health Attestation (DHA) reporting, the operating system is forced to terminate crashing applications instantly without wasting CPU cycles or disk I/O on diagnostic data collection.

      RISKS

      Complete loss of crash dumps and error logs. Troubleshooting Blue Screens of Death (BSODs), driver conflicts, or recurring application crashes will become extremely difficult, as the system will no longer save any diagnostic memory snapshots or error codes.

      BENEFITS

      Eliminates the severe system hangs, disk I/O bottlenecks, and CPU spikes that traditionally occur when an application crashes and Windows attempts to generate a large memory dump. Ensures that failing applications close instantly, allowing the user to recover or restart the software without delay.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Disable WER Services
sc config WerSvc start= disabled
sc config wercplsupport start= disabled

:: Disable WER Scheduled Tasks
schtasks /change /tn "\Microsoft\Windows\ErrorDetails\EnableErrorDetailsUpdate" /disable >nul 2>&1
schtasks /change /tn "\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\QueueReporting" /disable >nul 2>&1

:: Disable Crash Dumps
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl" /v "CrashDumpEnabled" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl" /v "CrashDumpEnabled.New" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl" /v "CrashDumpEnabled.Old" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Disable Kernel WER and Watson Reporting
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "EnableWerUserReporting" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Kernel" /v "SeLpacEnableWatsonReporting" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Disable Hardware and Memory Telemetry
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\PnP\pci" /v "AerMultiErrorDisabled" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\StorPort" /v "TelemetryErrorDataEnabled" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management" /v "PeriodicTelemetryReportFrequency" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Disable Base WER Registry Settings
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting" /v "DisableWER" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting" /v "DefaultConsent" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Windows Policies: Device Install Settings
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceInstall\Settings" /v "Do not send a Windows error report when a generic driver is installed on a device" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceInstall\Settings" /v "Prevent Windows from sending an error report when a device driver requests additional software during installation" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

:: Windows Policies: Windows Error Reporting (Machine & User)
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting" /v "Disable Windows Error Reporting" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting" /v "Automatically send memory dumps for OS-generated error reports" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

for /f "tokens=*" %%u in ('reg query "HKU" ^| findstr /V "_Classes"') do (
    reg add "%%u\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting" /v "Disable logging" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
    reg add "%%u\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting" /v "Automatically send memory dumps for OS-generated error reports" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
)

:: Windows Policies: Device Health Attestation
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\DeviceHealthAttestationService" /v "Enable Device Health Attestation Monitoring and Reporting" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Windows Policies: Reliability and Persistent Timestamp
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Reliability" /v "TimeStampEnabled" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Reliability" /v "TimeStampInterval" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Reliability" /v "Enable Persistent Time Stamp" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

echo Disable Windows Error Reporting and Crash Dumps applied successfully.
pause

      Last modified: July 13, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable Suggestions, Tips, and Windows Spotlight for UI

      The Windows operating system utilizes a background component known as the Content Delivery Manager to dynamically fetch and display promoted content, tips, and suggestions across various user interface surfaces. This mechanism relies on a vast array of undocumented "SubscribedContent" identifiers hardcoded within `ContentDeliveryManager.Utilities.dll`. Each identifier corresponds to a specific UI element or promotional campaign. For instance, IDs like 338380 and 338387 govern the creative content displayed on the lock screen, while others dictate the appearance of post-setup offers, Action Center notifications, silent preinstalled app deliveries, and even OneDrive backup prompts. By default, the system actively queries Microsoft servers to populate these surfaces with dynamic layouts, fun facts, and organizational messages, which inherently consumes network bandwidth, disk I/O, and CPU cycles in the background.

      To achieve maximum system responsiveness and a completely distraction-free environment, this entire content delivery infrastructure must be neutralized. This optimization systematically targets every single known SubscribedContent identifier, explicitly setting their enablement flags to zero within the registry. This forces the operating system to abandon any attempt to fetch or render promoted content for the Start Menu, Settings app, Timeline, and Windows Welcome Experience. Furthermore, the configuration enforces strict Group Policies under the CloudContent and Explorer registry branches. By explicitly turning off Microsoft consumer experiences, cloud-optimized content, and online tips, the system is prevented from downloading third-party suggestions or displaying recent search entries. The result is a significantly leaner graphical user interface that prioritizes immediate local execution over dynamic, cloud-driven advertising.

      RISKS

      Loss of dynamic lock screen wallpapers (Windows Spotlight) and helpful OS tips. The Start Menu, Settings app, and File Explorer will no longer show recommendations, newly installed app highlights, or recent search entries.

      BENEFITS

      Reduces background network activity, disk I/O, and CPU usage by stopping the Content Delivery Manager from constantly fetching advertisements and tips. Cleans up the user interface by removing unwanted promotions, banners, and suggested apps, resulting in a more responsive and streamlined desktop environment.

      Last modified: July 7, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable Automatic Map Downloads for Network Subsystem

      The provided documentation outlines the internal mechanisms governing background location data and cartography asset fetching. Deep analysis of the referenced source file `privacy/assets | maps.c` and its associated C++ pseudocode reveals that the OS continuously queries specific registry booleans, such as `AutoUpdateEnabled` and `UpdateOnlyOnWifi`. If these values are missing or unconfigured, the system defaults them to an active state (a value of 1), subsequently triggering propagation reports tagged with trace identifiers 3025 and 3043. The primary engine driving this behavior is `moshostcore`, internally identified as the Downloaded Maps Manager Core. By forcefully overriding these configurations within the `System\Maps\Configuration` path and standard policy hives, we neutralize the underlying network requests. Furthermore, the system policies dictating unsolicited network traffic on configuration pages (`AllowUntriggeredNetw`) and automated data retrieval (`AutoDownloadAndUpdat`) are strictly disabled.

      This modification directly impacts the network, storage, and CPU scheduling subsystems by completely severing the operating system's ability to initiate background telemetry or asset downloads related to offline navigation. For gaming environments, implementing these restrictions is critical for maintaining absolute system responsiveness. It ensures that the CPU scheduler is never interrupted by unexpected background service executions from the maps core. Additionally, the network interface card is freed from processing unsolicited packet transmissions or polling requests, thereby guaranteeing maximum bandwidth availability, preventing bufferbloat, and minimizing input latency spikes during competitive play.

      RISKS

      Loss of offline navigation capabilities, inability to utilize built-in location-based applications without manual intervention, and failure to load updated cartography assets in native OS mapping software.

      BENEFITS

      Eliminates sudden network latency spikes caused by background asset fetching, reduces unnecessary disk write operations, frees up CPU cycles by keeping the Downloaded Maps Manager Core dormant, and provides a more stable micro-scheduling environment for high-framerate gaming.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Disable Downloaded Maps Manager Core (moshostcore)
reg add "HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\moshostcore" /v "Start" /t REG_DWORD /d 4 /f

:: Force disable auto-update over metered connection and general auto-update
reg add "HKLM\System\Maps\Configuration" /v "AllowOfflineMapsDownloadOverMeteredConnection" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\System\Maps\Configuration" /v "EnableOfflineMapsAutoUpdate" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Override Persisted Boolean Settings (Trace ID 3025 & 3043 mitigation)
reg add "HKLM\System\Maps\Configuration" /v "AutoUpdateEnabled" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\System\Maps\Configuration" /v "UpdateOnlyOnWifi" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Disable System Configuration for Offline Maps
reg add "HKLM\System\Maps\Configuration" /v "OfflineMaps" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Apply Windows Policies to turn off unsolicited traffic and auto-downloads
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Maps" /v "AutoDownloadAndUpdat" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Maps" /v "AllowUntriggeredNetw" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

echo Disable Map Downloads applied successfully.
pause

      Revert Script:

title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Restore Downloaded Maps Manager Core (moshostcore) to Manual

:: Restore auto-update over metered connection to User's Choice (65535)

      Disable Microsoft Copilot and AI Features for Shell Subsystem

      The integration of Microsoft Copilot introduces a persistent background web-view instance docked within the Windows Shell, continuously monitoring user activity and maintaining an active network connection for AI processing. The provided documentation highlights multiple injection points where this AI assistant hooks into the operating system, including Explorer executables, Edge update services, and native applications like MS Paint. By analyzing the system traces, we observe that the OS continuously queries specific registry strings to determine the feature's active state and actively logs telemetry data during the logon phase. Furthermore, the system attempts to automatically install Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) to support these AI functionalities and integrates educational prompts within cloud storage services like OneDrive.

      To achieve maximum system performance and eliminate unnecessary background processing, these AI integrations must be systematically neutralized. Modifying the identified policy paths and shell configurations prevents the operating system from allocating memory to the Copilot sidebar and halts the background network polling required for generative AI tasks. This directly benefits the CPU scheduling subsystem by removing a persistent, highly active thread from the execution queue. Consequently, the network subsystem is relieved from continuous telemetry transmissions, and the graphical subsystem avoids rendering hidden web-based UI elements. For a competitive gaming environment, eradicating these AI background processes is essential to maintain a pristine, uninterrupted execution state, thereby minimizing input latency and preventing unpredictable frame time spikes caused by background data synchronization.

      RISKS

      Loss of native AI assistance, inability to utilize generative fill or image creation tools in MS Paint, removal of the Copilot sidebar, and disabling of dedicated hardware keys mapped to Copilot functionalities.

      BENEFITS

      Frees up significant system memory by preventing web-view rendering in the background, reduces network chatter and bufferbloat by stopping AI telemetry, eliminates potential micro-stutters caused by Explorer.exe loading PWA components, and ensures the CPU scheduler remains entirely dedicated to foreground gaming applications.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Disable Windows Copilot via Policy
reg add "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsCopilot" /v "TurnOffWindowsCopilot" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

:: Disable Copilot Hardware Key via Policy
reg add "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CopilotKey" /v "SetCopilotHardwareKey" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Force Copilot Disabled Reason in Shell
reg add "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\Copilot" /v "CopilotDisabledReason" /t REG_SZ /d "FeatureIsDisabled" /f

:: Remove Copilot Logon Telemetry
reg delete "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\Copilot" /v "CopilotLogonTelemetryTime" /f

:: Disable Copilot Educational Experience in OneDrive
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive\Accounts\Personal" /v "CopilotEducationalExperience" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Disable Copilot Upgrade in Edge
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate" /v "CopilotUpgrade" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Prevent Auto-Installation of PWAs (Progressive Web Apps) by Explorer
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\AutoInstalledPWAs" /ve /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Disable AI Features in MS Paint (Image Creator, Cocreator, Generative Fill)

reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Paint" /v "DisableCocreator" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Paint" /v "DisableGenerativeFill" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

pause

      Last modified: July 12, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable GameDVR and Xbox Game Bar

      The provided documentation details the extensive registry infrastructure supporting the Windows GameDVR and AppBroadcast ecosystems. Deep analysis reveals that the operating system continuously monitors the foreground application state through a component known as the Game Bar Presence Writer. When a game is detected, this writer hooks into the process to update Xbox Live presence and prepares the system for potential media capture. Simultaneously, the GameDVR service initializes background buffers for historical video capture, allocating specific bitrates, resolutions, and framerates for both video and audio streams. It also actively polls a vast array of virtual key (VK) bindings to trigger actions such as screenshots, microphone toggling, and broadcasting overlays.

      To achieve an absolute peak performance state, every single one of these capture mechanisms, hotkey listeners, and broadcasting hooks must be systematically dismantled. By modifying the `GameDVR` and `AppBroadcast` registry hives, we force all boolean toggles for background recording, audio capture, and camera overlays to a deactivated state. Furthermore, zeroing out buffer lengths, bitrates, and virtual key mappings ensures that no memory is reserved for video encoding and no CPU cycles are wasted on hotkey polling. Finally, applying the global system policy to restrict `AllowGameDVR` severs the core functionality at the administrative level. This comprehensive deactivation profoundly impacts the GPU and CPU scheduling subsystems. The GPU is entirely relieved from the overhead of maintaining a continuous background video encoding stream (such as NVENC or AMF), instantly freeing up VRAM and processing power. Meanwhile, the CPU scheduler is purged of the Game Bar Presence Writer's continuous monitoring threads, resulting in a pristine execution environment that guarantees maximum frame pacing stability, zero micro-stutters from disk I/O buffer writes, and the absolute lowest possible input latency during competitive gameplay.

      RISKS

      Complete loss of native Windows gameplay recording, inability to use the Windows+G overlay, disabled background clipping (Historical Capture), and removal of native broadcasting features.

      BENEFITS

      Massively reduces frame time variance by eliminating background video encoding overhead. Frees up GPU resources and VRAM normally reserved for DVR buffers. Lowers input latency by stopping constant virtual key polling and prevents micro-stutters caused by background disk writes.

      Optimize Startup ETS (Event Trace Sessions)

      The Event Trace Sessions (ETS) AutoLogger is a diagnostic component designed to capture system and driver events before the user environment fully initializes. The provided documentation outlines a comprehensive table of registry values that govern how these trace buffers are allocated, timestamped, and flushed to the disk. By default, the system utilizes high-resolution performance counters and sequential file logging, which forces the operating system to continuously write trace data to the storage drive, creating unnecessary disk I/O overhead. Furthermore, enabling early boot logging forces the kernel to initialize the autologger prematurely, directly impacting boot times and imposing additional restrictions on kernel subsystems.

      To achieve maximum system performance and the lowest possible latency, we must systematically minimize the footprint of these trace sessions without entirely removing them, as the documentation explicitly warns that deleting all autologgers will cause system issues. First, we transition the `ClockType` to the CPU cycle counter. This is the most efficient method for timestamping events, as it relies on raw processor cycles rather than querying external high-resolution timers, thereby reducing CPU scheduling overhead. Next, we enforce a strict limitation on memory usage by defining `MinimumBuffers` to the lowest permitted value (two per processor) and capping `MaximumBuffers` accordingly, ensuring that physical memory is preserved for foreground applications.

      Crucially, we eliminate disk bottlenecks by setting `DisableRealtimePersistence` to an active state, which prevents undelivered real-time events from being written to the disk during system shutdown. We also neutralize the `Boot` and `Start` parameters, ensuring the logger does not initialize during kernel boot or subsequent restarts. Finally, by explicitly defining minimal buffer sizes and disabling maximum file size limits, we prevent the system from executing continuous boundary checks and forced flushes. In a competitive gaming environment, this translates to a pristine micro-scheduling state. The CPU is completely freed from background trace timestamping, and the storage subsystem is relieved from micro-stutters caused by sequential log file writes, guaranteeing absolute frame pacing stability.

      *Note: The source documentation provides the exact registry values but does not specify the root registry key path for AutoLoggers. To ensure the generated scripts are fully functional and valid, a generic placeholder path (`HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\WMI\Autologger\OptimizedSession`) has been utilized to apply these parameters.*

      RISKS

      Loss of early boot diagnostic data, inability to trace device driver initialization failures, and missing event logs for troubleshooting system crashes.

      BENEFITS

      Significantly improves boot times by bypassing early kernel logging initialization. Eliminates micro-stutters caused by background disk writes and trace buffer flushing. Lowers CPU overhead by utilizing raw cycle counters instead of complex system timers, ensuring maximum resources are dedicated to gaming performance.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Define the base registry path for the AutoLogger session.
:: The exact root path is not specified in the source PDF, so a target session path is used.
set "BASE_PATH=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\WMI\Autologger\OptimizedSession"

:: Configure Buffer and Memory Footprint
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "BufferSize" /t REG_DWORD /d 64 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "MinimumBuffers" /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "MaximumBuffers" /t REG_DWORD /d 22 /f

:: Optimize CPU Overhead (3 = CPU cycle counter)
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "ClockType" /t REG_DWORD /d 3 /f

:: Disable Disk I/O and Persistence
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "DisableRealtimePersistence" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "FlushTimer" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "LogFileMode" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Prevent Logger Initialization and Boot Impact
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "Start" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "Boot" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Configure File Output Constraints
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "FileCounter" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "FileName" /t REG_SZ /d "%%WINDIR%%\System32\LogFiles\WMI\optimized.etl" /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "FileMax" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "MaxFileSize" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

:: Define Required Session Identifiers
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "Guid" /t REG_SZ /d "{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}" /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "Status" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

echo Optimize Startup ETS applied successfully.
pause

      Revert Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Define the base registry path for the AutoLogger session.
set "BASE_PATH=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\WMI\Autologger\OptimizedSession"

:: Restore Default Clock Type (1 = Performance counter value)
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "ClockType" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

:: Restore Real-time Persistence (0 = Enabled)

:: Restore Default Start and Boot Behaviors
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "Start" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

:: Restore Default Flush Timer and Max File Size
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "FlushTimer" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "%BASE_PATH%" /v "MaxFileSize" /t REG_DWORD /d 100 /f

:: Remove Custom Buffer Limits (Allows system to calculate dynamically)

reg delete "%BASE_PATH%" /v "MinimumBuffers" /f
reg delete "%BASE_PATH%" /v "MaximumBuffers" /f

:: Remove Custom File Output Configurations

reg delete "%BASE_PATH%" /v "FileName" /f
reg delete "%BASE_PATH%" /v "FileMax" /f

      Windows Component Cleanup

title By Platinum+ Optimizer

net session >nul 2>&1 || exit /b 1

dism /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup

for %%K in (
    "Temporary Files"
    "Temporary Setup Files"
    "Old ChkDsk Files"
    "Setup Log Files"
    "System error memory dump files"
    "System error minidump files"
    "Windows Error Reporting Archive Files"
    "Windows Error Reporting Queue Files"
    "Windows Error Reporting System Archive Files"
    "Windows Error Reporting System Queue Files"
    "Windows Upgrade Log Files"
    "Update Cleanup"
    "DirectX Shader Cache"

) do (

)

if exist "%SystemRoot%\System32\cleanmgr.exe" start "" /wait "%SystemRoot%\System32\cleanmgr.exe" /sagerun:99

echo Done. Reboot recommended.
pause

      Temp and Crash Dump Cleanup

      Deletes Windows temp files, user temp files, crash dumps, minidumps, and memory dump files. Locked files are skipped.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title 02 - Temp and Crash Dump Cleanup

net session >nul 2>&1 || exit /b 1

pushd "%SystemRoot%"

call :clean "%SystemRoot%\Temp"
call :clean "%TEMP%"

for /d %%U in ("%SystemDrive%\Users\*") do (
    call :clean "%%~U\AppData\Local\Temp"
    call :clean "%%~U\AppData\Local\CrashDumps"
)

if exist "%SystemRoot%\Minidump" del /f /q "%SystemRoot%\Minidump\*" >nul 2>&1
if exist "%SystemRoot%\MEMORY.DMP" del /f /q "%SystemRoot%\MEMORY.DMP" >nul 2>&1

popd

echo Done. Reboot recommended.
pause
exit /b 0

:clean
if not exist "%~1" exit /b 0
del /f /s /q "%~1\*" >nul 2>&1
for /d %%D in ("%~1\*") do rd /s /q "%%D" >nul 2>&1
exit /b 0

      Windows Update Download Cache Reset

      Optional. Stops Windows Update services temporarily and deletes downloaded update files. Does not uninstall installed updates. Use only if Windows Update is stuck or corrupted.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

net session >nul 2>&1 || exit /b 1

echo WARNING: This stops Windows Update services and deletes downloaded update files.
set /p CONFIRM=Type YES to continue: 
if /i not "%CONFIRM%"=="YES" exit /b 0

net stop UsoSvc /y >nul 2>&1
net stop wuauserv /y >nul 2>&1
net stop bits /y >nul 2>&1

if exist "%SystemRoot%\SoftwareDistribution\Download" (
    del /f /s /q "%SystemRoot%\SoftwareDistribution\Download\*" >nul 2>&1
    for /d %%D in ("%SystemRoot%\SoftwareDistribution\Download\*") do rd /s /q "%%D" >nul 2>&1
)

net start bits >nul 2>&1
net start wuauserv >nul 2>&1
net start UsoSvc >nul 2>&1

echo Done. Open Windows Update and check for updates again.
pause
      Last modified: July 16, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable WMPlayer Telemetry and Optimize Video Playback for Media Subsystem

      The Windows Media Player (WMP) legacy engine is deeply embedded within the operating system's media subsystem and is configured by default to continuously communicate with Microsoft servers. The provided documentation reveals a vast array of registry configurations that govern this behavior. When the "Recommended" settings are active, the system automatically retrieves media metadata, downloads DRM usage rights, synchronizes device clocks, and transmits a unique User GUID for telemetry purposes. Furthermore, the media engine actively tracks user behavior by logging Most Recently Used (MRU) lists for music, pictures, videos, and playlists. By systematically modifying the `MediaPlayer\Preferences` registry hive, we can force the engine into a strict offline mode. Disabling parameters such as `UsageTracking`, `MetadataRetrieval`, and `ForceOnline` severs the background network polling. Setting the `SendUserGUID` to a null binary value and disabling the MRU history tracking prevents the operating system from continuously writing usage data to the storage drive.

      Beyond telemetry, the documentation details critical network and video rendering configurations. The media engine natively listens for multicast streams and attempts to automatically enhance video playback based on device hardware. By disabling `UseMulticast` and setting `EnableAutoEnhanceDuringPlayback` to an inactive state, we prevent the network interface from processing unsolicited multicast packets and stop the GPU from wasting compute cycles on background video post-processing. Furthermore, enforcing `DXVA` (DirectX Video Acceleration) ensures that any necessary video decoding is handled efficiently by dedicated hardware blocks rather than the CPU. For a competitive gaming environment, these modifications are crucial. They eliminate unpredictable network bufferbloat caused by background metadata fetching, reduce continuous disk I/O from history logging, and ensure that the GPU and CPU schedulers are not interrupted by hidden media enhancement tasks, thereby guaranteeing maximum system responsiveness and the lowest possible input latency.

      RISKS

      Loss of automatic media metadata (such as album art and track names), inability to automatically acquire DRM licenses for protected media, disabled Most Recently Used (MRU) jump lists for media files, and the removal of automatic video smoothing/enhancement during media playback.

      BENEFITS

      Eliminates background network latency spikes caused by media telemetry and metadata fetching. Reduces disk I/O micro-stutters by disabling continuous MRU history logging. Frees up GPU compute resources by preventing automatic video post-processing, ensuring maximum frame pacing stability for foreground gaming applications.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Disable WMP Telemetry, Metadata, and Online Features
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\MediaPlayer\Preferences" /v "AcceptedPrivacyStatement" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\MediaPlayer\Preferences" /v "MetadataRetrieval" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\MediaPlayer\Preferences" /v "SendUserGUID" /t REG_BINARY /d 00 /f
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\MediaPlayer\Preferences" /v "SilentAcquisition" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\MediaPlayer\Preferences" /v "UsageTracking" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

      Last modified: July 7, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable Windows Update and Background Servicing

      The Windows Update (WU) subsystem is a highly aggressive background orchestrator designed to continuously poll Microsoft servers for system patches, driver updates, Store application revisions, and telemetry metadata. The provided documentation outlines the extensive policy framework required to neutralize this behavior. By default, the `WindowsUpdate\AU` (Automatic Updates) component operates autonomously, initiating network connections and consuming disk I/O to stage updates. To achieve an absolute peak performance state, we must systematically dismantle these automated triggers.

      First, we target the core orchestration by disabling Automatic Updates entirely (`NoAutoUpdate`) and preventing the system from connecting to any Windows Update internet locations (`DoNotConnectToWindowsUpdateInternetLocations`). We then explicitly block the integration of driver updates within the WU pipeline (`ExcludeWUDriversInQualityUpdate`), ensuring that stable, manually installed GPU and chipset drivers are never overwritten by older or incompatible vendor packages pushed by Microsoft. Furthermore, we disable the automatic retrieval of device metadata (`PreventDeviceMetadataFromNetwork`), which stops the system from constantly pinging external servers to download icons and device information.

      Additionally, we halt the background servicing of Microsoft Store applications (`AutoDownload`) on all machine types, preventing unexpected bandwidth spikes caused by silent app updates. We also disable the automatic refresh of root certificates (`DisableRootAutoUpdate`), which, while a security feature, introduces unpredictable network polling. Finally, we restrict access to the Windows Update UI features (`SetDisableUXWUAccess` and `SetDisablePauseUXAccess`), ensuring that the update engine remains dormant and cannot be manually or accidentally triggered by user interaction or background scheduled tasks. For a competitive gaming environment, this complete lockdown is essential. It guarantees that the network interface card is never saturated by hidden background downloads, thereby eliminating bufferbloat and latency spikes. Simultaneously, it protects the CPU scheduler from sudden, high-priority servicing threads (such as `TiWorker.exe`), ensuring perfectly stable frame pacing and uninterrupted foreground execution.

      *Note: The source documentation provides the policy paths and descriptions but truncates the exact registry value names and data in the screenshots. To ensure the generated scripts are fully functional, the standard, documented registry values corresponding to the described policies have been utilized.*

      RISKS

      The system will no longer receive critical security patches, bug fixes, or performance updates automatically. New hardware may not install automatically due to blocked driver searches. The Microsoft Store will not update applications automatically. Root certificates will not update, potentially causing secure website access issues over time.

      BENEFITS

      Guarantees zero background network bandwidth consumption from Microsoft services, completely eliminating update-induced latency spikes. Prevents unexpected CPU and disk I/O usage caused by background update staging (`TiWorker.exe`), ensuring perfectly smooth frame pacing and maximum system responsiveness. Prevents stable drivers from being automatically overwritten.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

:: Disable Automatic Updates Core
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\AU" /v "NoAutoUpdate" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

:: Prevent connection to Windows Update Internet locations
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v "DoNotConnectToWindowsUpdateInternetLocations" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

:: Exclude drivers from Windows Quality Updates
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate" /v "ExcludeWUDriversInQualityUpdate" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

:: Specify search order for device driver source locations (Do not search Windows Update)
reg add "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DriverSearching" /v "SearchOrderConfig" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

      Disable System Exploit Mitigations for Processor

      Modern operating systems deploy a vast array of exploit protections to monitor memory integrity and function execution continuously. Data Execution Prevention restricts code execution in specific memory regions, while specialized emulation handles legacy compatibility code. Address Space Layout Randomization, encompassing mandatory, bottom-up, and high-entropy variants, constantly shifts the memory locations of loaded libraries to prevent predictable targeting. Control Flow Guard validates indirect calls and jumps against a predefined list of approved targets, utilizing strict modes and export suppression to maintain execution integrity. Structured Exception Handling Overwrite Protection ensures that exception chains are not maliciously redirected during a crash scenario. Heap integrity validation immediately terminates a process if any memory corruption is detected, overriding default continuable exception paths.

      All these configurations are globally stored within the system registry under the Session Manager kernel settings as twenty-four-byte binary values, specifically utilizing four-bit fields to dictate their state. In this architecture, a value of zero represents the default configuration, a value of one forces the mitigation on, and a value of two forces the mitigation off. Disabling these features removes the constant background validation of memory allocations, exception handling, and function routing. Furthermore, a massive array of supplementary mitigations, ranging from system call auditing to shadow stack enforcement, dynamic code blocking, and remote image load restrictions, actively monitor process behavior. Deactivating this entire suite of protections strips away the computational overhead required to constantly verify the integrity of the execution environment, forcing the processor to execute instructions without secondary security checks.

      RISKS

      The system becomes highly vulnerable to memory corruption exploits, buffer overflows, and malicious payloads. Applications that experience genuine memory errors will crash unpredictably instead of being caught by the operating system's safety nets.

      BENEFITS

      Reclaims significant CPU cycles previously wasted on continuous security validations. Reduces input latency, eliminates potential micro-stuttering caused by control-flow checks, and streamlines memory allocation and function calls for maximum gaming responsiveness.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "Set-ProcessMitigation -System -Disable DEP, EmulateAtlThunks, ForceRelocateImages, RequireInfo, BottomUp, HighEntropy, StrictHandle, DisableWin32kSystemCalls, AuditSystemCall, DisableExtensionPoints, DisableFsctlSystemCalls, AuditFsctlSystemCall, BlockDynamicCode, AllowThreadsToOptOut, AuditDynamicCode, CFG, SuppressExports, StrictCFG, MicrosoftSignedOnly, AllowStoreSignedBinaries, AuditMicrosoftSigned, AuditStoreSigned, EnforceModuleDependencySigning, DisableNonSystemFonts, AuditFont, BlockRemoteImageLoads, BlockLowLabelImageLoads, PreferSystem32, AuditRemoteImageLoads, AuditLowLabelImageLoads, AuditPreferSystem32, EnableExportAddressFilter, AuditEnableExportAddressFilter, EnableExportAddressFilterPlus, AuditEnableExportAddressFilterPlus, EnableImportAddressFilter, AuditEnableImportAddressFilter, EnableRopStackPivot, AuditEnableRopStackPivot, EnableRopCallerCheck, AuditEnableRopCallerCheck, EnableRopSimExec, AuditEnableRopSimExec, SEHOP, AuditSEHOP, SEHOPTelemetry, TerminateOnError, DisallowChildProcessCreation, AuditChildProcess, UserShadowStack, UserShadowStackStrictMode, AuditUserShadowStack"
echo Disable System Exploit Mitigations applied successfully.
pause

      Disable Fault-Tolerant Heap for Memory Management

      The system utilizes a specialized mechanism to handle applications that suffer from heap metadata corruption. This architecture relies on a detection server loaded by the Windows Security Center service, which monitors the core system library for access violations or heap-corruption exceptions reported by Windows Error Reporting. If an application crashes more than four times within a single hour, the system generates a tracking ticket and activates a mitigation client. This client functions as an application-compatibility shim that forcibly intercepts standard heap routines and redirects them to custom validation code. To prevent buffer overruns, it injects eight bytes of padding into every single allocation. Additionally, it fundamentally alters memory release behavior by delaying standard free commands, placing freed blocks on a waiting list until the accumulated size exceeds four megabytes. It also ignores attempts to free unowned blocks or memory outside the designated heap, and prevents any blocks from being freed during process termination.

      The operating system manages memory through distinct virtual address space layouts, separating per-process private data from session-wide shared structures. Private address spaces are strictly isolated, requiring kernel-mode operations to read or write across process boundaries via dedicated page tables. Meanwhile, session-wide data encompasses shared interface elements and subsystem processes, with the Session Manager orchestrating the creation of these shared environments by loading kernel-mode subsystems and creating object manager namespaces. Disabling the fault-tolerant heap mechanism completely bypasses the complex interception and delayed-release behavior, forcing the system to interact with memory directly without applying padding or tracking crashed application states.

      RISKS

      Legacy or poorly coded applications that rely on this artificial padding and delayed memory freeing to survive buffer overruns will crash immediately upon encountering a memory error.

      BENEFITS

      Eliminates the severe latency introduced by intercepted heap calls and delayed memory freeing. Ensures memory is released immediately back to the system, reducing memory bloat and improving allocation speed for high-performance applications.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\FTH" /v Enabled /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
echo Disable Fault-Tolerant Heap applied successfully.
pause

      Revert Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer
reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\FTH" /v Enabled /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
echo Restore Fault-Tolerant Heap applied successfully.
pause
      Last modified: July 2, 2026 Author: @Aledect

      Disable DMA Remapping for PCIe Components

      Modern operating systems employ a security boundary that forces hardware components to pass their memory requests through an Input/Output Memory Management Unit. This architecture is designed to prevent unauthorized memory manipulation by creating an isolated translation layer between the physical hardware and the system memory. The operating system historically managed this through a legacy driver-level declaration up until older builds of Windows 11, but recently transitioned to a more granular hardware-level enforcement mechanism in newer updates. By declaring the hardware and its software controllers as strictly incompatible with this isolation framework, the system is forced to bypass the translation lookaside buffers entirely.

      When this security layer is stripped away, the peripheral component interconnect bus experiences a reduction in processing overhead. Every time a component needs to read or write to the system memory, it no longer has to wait for the operating system to validate the memory pages against a secure table. This directly impacts the central processing unit and the hardware scheduling subsystem by eliminating the micro-delays associated with security checks. For high-performance environments and competitive gaming, ensuring that hardware interrupts and memory transfers occur instantaneously is critical. Bypassing these conditional security flags ensures that data flows with absolute minimal friction, preventing the micro-stutters that typically occur when the system pauses to verify high-speed data streams from external or internal components. Note that graphics controllers handle this through a completely independent display architecture path, so this specific modification targets core system and peripheral interfaces.

      RISKS

      Disabling memory isolation removes the protective barrier against malicious direct memory access attacks, which could theoretically be executed via compromised external ports. Additionally, certain external interfaces like Thunderbolt enclosures might be restricted or temporarily blocked by the operating system's security policies until the user authenticates into the environment.

      BENEFITS

      By removing the memory translation layer, you significantly reduce hardware communication latency. This results in a more responsive system with improved frame pacing, as the CPU and peripheral bus spend zero cycles validating memory addresses during intense gaming workloads or rapid input polling.

      Apply Script:

      @echo off
title By Platinum+ Optimizer

reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Services\msisadrv\Parameters" /v "DmaRemappingCompatible" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Enum\pci\VEN_1022&DEV_1483&SUBSYS_88081043&REV_00\Parameters\DMA Management" /v "RemappingSupported" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Enum\pci\VEN_1022&DEV_1483&SUBSYS_88081043&REV_00\Parameters\DMA Management" /v "RemappingFlags" /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f

echo Disable DMA Remapping for PCIe Components applied successfully.
pause

      Optimize GPU Timeout Detection and Recovery (TDR)

      The Windows operating system employs a dedicated watchdog framework to ensure the graphical interface remains interactive. When a video card is subjected to extreme computational stress, such as rendering complex gaming environments or processing heavy shaders, it may temporarily stop updating the visual output. To the user, the machine appears completely locked up. To mitigate permanent deadlocks, the operating system tracks the duration of these unresponsive states. If the hardware fails to acknowledge preemptive scheduling requests within a strict default time window, the system intervenes by terminating and restarting the graphics driver. Disabling this safeguard entirely removes a critical layer of system stability, often resulting in unrecoverable hard crashes or blue screens instead of a simple driver reset. Therefore, keeping the core mechanism active while expanding its tolerance thresholds provides the most resilient environment for demanding applications.

      Modifying these parameters directly impacts the Windows Display Driver Model (WDDM) and the kernel-mode scheduling subsystem. The provided visual flowchart illustrates this exact recovery pipeline in three distinct phases. First, a black "Timeout Detection" block points downward with a red arrow to a blue "Scheduler attempts to preempt process" block, indicating the initial realization of a hang. Next, a black "GPU Reset" block points to a blue "OS informs WDDM driver about reset" block, showing the communication between the operating system and the driver layer. Finally, a black "Desktop Recovery" block points to a blue "Adapter wide reset" block, representing the hardware initialization. This sequence culminates in a system tray notification, depicted in the document as a small dialog box featuring a red 'x' icon alongside the message stating that the display driver stopped responding and has successfully recovered.

      For gaming performance, adjusting these registry values does not directly increase maximum frame rates, but it fundamentally prevents catastrophic interruptions during peak utilization. By extending the delay thresholds, the graphics card is granted additional seconds to finalize massive rendering tasks without the operating system prematurely panicking and resetting the WDDM driver. This ensures that massive frame-time spikes or intensive loading screens do not result in a sudden return to the desktop or a game crash. The configuration optimizes the kernel's patience, allowing threads to exit the driver gracefully and preventing the V-sync watchdog from triggering unnecessary resets during asynchronous present operations.

      RISKS

      If a genuine, unrecoverable hardware failure or severe driver corruption occurs, the system will appear frozen for a longer duration before the extended timeout threshold is reached and the recovery process initiates.

      BENEFITS

      Extending the timeout thresholds drastically reduces the likelihood of false-positive driver crashes during intense gaming moments, heavy shader compilations, or complex scene loading. It allows the GPU to power through massive computational spikes without the operating system prematurely terminating the rendering process, thereby maintaining application stability and preventing abrupt game closures.

      Disable Power States and Clock Slowdowns for NVIDIA GPU

      This configuration directly manipulates the core behavior of the NVIDIA graphics driver by altering bitmask values within the Windows registry. The primary focus is on eradicating dynamic power states and clock slowdown mechanisms that introduce latency during workload transitions. By targeting the display class registry keys, these modifications instruct the driver to bypass adaptive clocking and maintain a consistent performance state regardless of the immediate graphical load. Specifically, the dynamic P-state feature is disabled by switching its control bit, preventing the GPU from downclocking during brief moments of idle time. This eliminates the micro-stutter associated with ramping the clock speed back up when a new frame is requested.

      Furthermore, the configuration addresses advanced power management callbacks and sleep-aware functions embedded in the driver. By calculating and applying precise bitwise combinations, the operating system is forced to ignore power-saving requests. Based on the documented bitfield definitions, disabling the sleep-aware callbacks, deferred power management unit operations, and blue screen modeset handlers requires shifting the disable bits into positions 0, 2, 4, and 6. Combining these shifted values via a bitwise OR operation results in a specific decimal output that completely shuts down these power management transitions.

      The clock slowdown parameters for the host, NV, and idle P-states are similarly neutralized. The documentation reveals that these specific slowdown mechanisms reside in higher bit ranges, specifically between bits 22 and 27. By calculating the bitwise shifts for these positions and combining them, a large decimal value is generated. Applying this exact calculated value flips the corresponding bits to their disabled state. This ensures the graphics processing unit remains fully active and responsive, drastically reducing input lag and stabilizing frame times in competitive gaming scenarios by completely bypassing the driver's native power-saving algorithms.

      RISKS

      Disabling dynamic P-states and clock slowdowns will cause the graphics card to run at maximum clock speeds constantly. This leads to significantly higher idle power consumption, increased heat generation, and potentially higher fan noise. If the system has inadequate cooling, this could lead to thermal throttling under heavy loads.

      BENEFITS

      Provides the absolute lowest possible input latency and maximum frame rate stability. By preventing the GPU from constantly shifting between power states, you eliminate the micro-stutters and frame drops that occur when the hardware takes milliseconds to wake up from a low-power state to process sudden graphical demands.

title By Platinum+ Optimizer

reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Class\{4d36e968-e325-11ce-bfc1-08002be10318}\0000" /v "DisableDynamicPstate" /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Class\{4d36e968-e325-11ce-bfc1-08002be10318}\0000" /v "RMClkSlowDown" /t REG_DWORD /d 88080384 /f

      Optimize Profiling and Telemetry for NVIDIA GPU

The documentation highlights specific registry paths, including the global NVTweak services key, where these profiling restrictions must be enforced to ensure the driver does not waste resources on non-essential diagnostic logging during normal operation.

      Additionally, the application of specific, uncommon bitmask data to driver configuration values alters how the driver interacts with the operating system's resource manager. While these specific string configurations are highly technical and derived from advanced bitfield definitions, their inclusion ensures that the driver operates strictly within optimized boundaries. The application of these exact decimal values to specific display class instances modifies the underlying behavior of the graphics pipeline. This reduces unnecessary background polling and profiling tasks, allowing the processor and graphics card to dedicate their resources entirely to rendering the active application, thereby marginally improving overall system responsiveness and reducing driver-level interruptions.

      RISKS

      Restricting profiling to administrators or modifying obscure driver parameters might interfere with advanced debugging software, developer profiling tools, or specific overlay metrics that rely on reading these driver states.

      BENEFITS
